speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the signing by the Queen of the proclamation bringing into force
Canada's new Constitution was of profound historic significance for all Canadians. The occasion marked the completion of the work toward full Canadian sovereignty launched by the Fathers of Confederation at their first meeting in Charlottetown in 1864. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley):
That the House supports the Prime Minister's statement in the House on Wednesday that active consideration should be given to making an official copy, with original signatures of the proclamation, to be placed in Province House at Charlottetown where the Fathers of Confederation held their historic meeting that gave birth to our great country.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR GLOBAL LIMITATION-MOTION UNDER S.O 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in light of the growing conviction of the peoples of the world that their respective governments need to know that they are concerned about the drift toward global nuclear death, and the insanity of anyone, even if he is a president, thinking that nuclear war is winnable, a concern demonstrated this week in North America by the grassroots movement Ground Zero, and by hundreds of thousands of Europeans earlier this year, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell):
That this House instructs the Prime Minister, (1) to show that he is serious about his nuclear suffocation strategy by cancelling the Cruise missile testing in Alberta; (2) to make Canada a leader rather than an acquiescent observer in the struggle for mutual arms limitations at the United Nations Special Session on Disarmament by, among other things, calling for a global referendum on disarmament and, (3) to withdraw our nuclear team from Argentina immediately and have the wisdom to reject finally all the ways in which Canada has been contributing to the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The government's refusal to take positive, sensible action to move the nation out of its recessive situation has resulted in the withering of our business base, and high levels of unemployment. That the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion implement at once the long-promised expansion of regional development incentive grants in Ontario, through the creation of new boundaries, or the enlargement of existing ones.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister in anticipation of his cabinet meeting this weekend. As the Prime Minister knows, in 1968 there were 358,000 Canadians out of work, which represented at that time 4.5 per cent of the labour force. Now 9 per cent of the labour force is out of work representing almost 1.25 million Canadians. Since the Prime Minister has been in office practically the entire time since 1968, would he explain to the House what he feels is the most significant reason why unemployment in percentage terms has doubled and, in real numbers has tripled since 1968?
[DOT] (U15)

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it would be difficult to point out the many economic reasons why this has happened. I believe the hon. member would be able to mount a list of his own, but it is obvious that one of the main causes is that Canada is an exporting country, a country which relies very heavily on international trade. Almost one third of our GNP depends upon international trade. Of course flowing from that is the fact that most of our markets are in as high or higher unemployment situations, which means that most purchasers of our goods, whether they be processed or raw materials, have economies which are as bad or worse than ours and therefore cannot buy our products. But because we are more dependent upon international trade than many other major countries, it affects us in a less controllable way. This is one of the reasons. There are many others.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister who cited world conditions as one of the contributing factors to rising unemployment. As the Prime Minister knows, in the Report of The Special Committee on a National Trading Corporation in June, 1981, it was pointed out that "between 1969 and 1979 Canada suffered a 33 per cent decline in its over-all share of world exports" and that "this performance was the worst among industrialized countries during this period." In view of the fact that the Prime Minister has been in power practically the entire time since 1969, how can he explain that our share of world trade has actually deteriorated to the point that, on manufactured goods, our deficit is now $16 billion higher than it was then, which represents something like 700,000 Canadians who are not working due to this deterioration in our share of world trade?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I find it difficult to understand the statistics put forward by the hon. member. I will look into them and perhaps be able to give a more precise or contradictory view of these statistics. They seem difficult to understand because in the last few years Canada has broken all previous records in its positive trade balance, in the sense that we have had larger positive trade balances in the last few years than we had at any previous time in our history. I will look into the statistical matter, but the hon. member draws attention to an important-
Raw materials.
Pardon?
Raw materials.

The hon. member draws attention to an important factor. There has been a worrisome trend in the productivity of the Canadian economy due to many factors, but this drop in productivity can explain that we are becoming less competitive in world markets and also the general disposition of Canadians not to take into account that the OPEC crisis of 1973 and its follow-up have made Canada a less fastgrowing country than in the past. This is something which much of our society is not prepared to accept. In other words, we have a tendency to live beyond our means and not to take into account the fact that we are not growing as fast and as rich as we were before the OPEC crisis.

Madam Speaker, again my question is directed to the Prime Minister. I would hope he might develop his last theme a little more, in that he indicated that our deterioration in productivity is due to the fact that we are living beyond our means. Would the Prime Minister indicate whether, if that is his rationalization for the figures

April 23, 1982
Oral Questions
given by his seatmate, the Minister of Finance, in last November's budget which, at page 4, made clear in "the current economic situation" brought out at that time, that Canada's growth in productivity from 1973 through to the present was one eighth of the growth experienced by the United Kingdom and Italy, and was compounded in the case of Japan, to a growth of 3.3 per cent, and in the case of France, to 2.5 per cent; only 0.2 per cent per annum, he is willing to stand up in the House and say that the only reason we ended up at the bottom of the list as compared to those other six countries listed by the Minister of Finance on productivity growth is that this nation has a tendency to live beyond its means and that his government's lack of direction to get us back to prosperity had nothing to do with it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, I did not link those two as cause to effect. I just indicated that these were two elements, that we had suffered a slower growth in productivity and we also had a tendency to live beyond our means. These were two of the causes but I did not link them causally. However, the reality is there.
The figure of the hon. member confirms what I said, and what the Minister of Finance has been saying. There is a worrisome loss of productivity per worker in Canada. I think that the hon. member is well enough versed in the subject to know that many economists who have studied this problem have not yet found an explanation for it. It is not such a simple-minded one as the hon. member gives when he says that the government has failed to give direction. It concerns the state and maturity of our economy, and our inventiveness or lack of it. It has to do with many factors, and it would be no cure to the current state of affairs to say that the government can change it all, unless the hon. member thinks that a socialist government which would direct everyone's lives should be in power, which is not my view.

Madam Speaker, my question is also to the Prime Minister. We now understand from department estimates that unemployment is expected to rise to 9.2 per cent in 1982. We hope that forecast is wrong. If we annualize the latest consumer price index, we see that inflation is running at 15.6 per cent. We hope that goes down. Interest rates remain unacceptably high, postal rates are rumoured to rise again, and our trade in manufactured end products-I stress "end products"-is in a massive deficit position. As well, gasoline is above two dollars a gallon and rising. We are paying 6 million dollars per day to subsidize imported oil while shutting down some of our own wells.
I ask the Prime Minister in all seriousness what people in the street are asking, and that is, does he really now what he is doing? That is what the people are asking. Is he waiting for a
miracle, and would it not be better for him and the country and all concerned if he resigns?

We happen to have a very distinguished minister from the French government in the gallery-

subsubtopic: ARGENTINA-SHIPMENT OF NUCLEAR FUEL FROM CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. On Monday in this House I asked a question of his Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. At that time I alleged that Argentina intended to divert plutonium from Canadian Candu reactors in order to make the bomb, or nuclear weapons. Now we find, according to a newspaper report today, that there is a government document in existence which states that Argentina was anything but stupid when it bought the reactor and that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources knew that fact. Can the Prime Minister confirm that an Ottawa firm has plans to ship $4.2 million worth of nuclear fuel to Argentina before the end of June, a fact which the government document states the government is anxious to hide?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ARGENTINA-SHIPMENT OF NUCLEAR FUEL FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as you know it is not my habit or custom to comment on so-called leaked cabinet documents. I consider that to be the best course of conduct and the only one in keeping with my oath of office.
In so far as the facts are concerned, I cannot comment on the particular ones mentioned by the hon. member, not having had enough time to read more than the headlines. However, I do know that we signed an agreement in 1976 or 1977 to build a Candu reactor in Argentina. That was done after we had
Oral Questions
obtained assurances from the Argentinians that full safeguards would be implemented in that country. That is the present situation. I imagine that we are discharging the other obligations under the contract, just as we expect them to discharge theirs.

subsubtopic: ARGENTINA-SHIPMENT OF NUCLEAR FUEL FROM CANADA
speechtext: I think that Britain was pretty sure, at one point, that Argentina would not invade the Falkland Islands, so perhaps the Prime Minister might want to reconsider its assurances.

Madam Speaker,
I would like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. Apparently this contract for $4.2 million involves 3,000 reactor fuel bundles. Given the fact that there seems to be a Canadian economic boycott against Argentina, will he assure this House that he will give instructions to stop this shipment to Argentina of the fuel bundles to which I have referred? If he is not prepared to give that assurance to the House now, will he please explain just exactly what is this economic boycott against Argentina?

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications, who will know that the arts and culture industries, like all sectors of our economy, are experiencing real difficulty this year. The government has hurt that sector on two fronts. First, it has reduced its year-over-year support for this sector in real dollar terms. Second, the budget seriously hurt investment in our arts and culture industries, particularly by its provisions for capital cost allowance and its attack on charitable foundations.
The minister has been travelling the country suggesting to those involved in one of our most important sectors that they can expect the new cultural initiative strategy to include serious new incentives for private investment in the arts and culture field. Can he tell this House and Canadians whether he has some foreknowledge that we are going to have a new minister of finance who will in fact respect the need for private investment in that sector, or will he admit that, when he tells Canadians there will be more private initiatives and private investment, he is kidding them?

Madam Speaker, I am delighted with this opportunity to answer the hon. member's question. Part of it is purely and stupidly political in the most partisan sense of the word. As for the serious part of his question in which he requested information on government support for arts and culture, I should like to remind the hon. member that this year we actually increased the federal contribution to the Canada Council. The hon. member may recall that only two or three weeks ago, we announced that we would be continuing the publishing assistance program which means another $25 million over three years for that sector.
The hon. member mentioned the matter of taxation and tax benefits. He knows as well as I do that there have been no changes in this area for the current year, and that the Minister of Finance has decided to postpone any changes in the area of tax incentives until next year. I also wish to point out that this year, under a program launched as part of the federal government's cultural initiatives strategy with the consent of all the provinces of Canada we on the federal side have been able to inject some $40 million over three years in the cultural sector, and if we add to this the contributions expected from the provinces and the private sector, it will mean an additional contribution of over $100 million for arts and culture over the next three years.

Madam Speaker, the minister has been better than some at delaying the attack by the Minister of Finance on this sector. He also knows that the estimates show that total government contributions to the arts this year, year-over-year, are 9.7 per cent over last year. The cabinet will be meeting this weekend at Meach Lake, presumably to discuss improvements to our economic circumstances. Will the minister tell this House what he is going to recommend to that minister on Sunday? For example, will we get a commitment that after five years of waiting for implementation of the Disney report, which is extremely important to the health and welfare of our artists, we will finally see its recommendations to relieve the tax burden on artists and important cultural people in this country, implemented?

Madam Speaker, I believe that the priority we give to cultural affairs is already a well-known fact, and I may add to my previous figures, which were actually too conservative, I must admit, that this year, the Government of Canada has announced it will spend a further $185 million, over four years, on the construction of a new national gallery and a new museum of man. The hon. member is well aware that a commission of inquiry is travelling across Canada, has held hearings and has even submitted a preliminary report. I am of course referring to the Applebaum-Hebert Commission. The hon. member himself has written to just about every single cultural organization in the country to complain that I was intending to take action before the report was published. Now he is asking me to divulge the recommendations that we as a department intend to make to the Minister of Finance or to other ministers in the Canadian government, and I am sure that if I gave him the answer he wanted, he would again say how awful it is that the minister responsible for cultural affairs in Parliament intends to take action before the Applebaum-Hebert report is tabled in the House. The hon. member should make up his mind what side of the fence he intends to be on during the months ahead.
April 23, 1982
The minister will be interested in knowing that the replies coming back to that letter suggest that his process is not trusted by the community.
What community?
The arts community which the minister claims to represent.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary to the minister is this. He has had five years to deal with issues such as the Disney report, issues which are supported by the community, issues on which they asked the minister to take action before the Applebaum-Hebert commission was started. Why does the minister continue to wait to take those actions to assist the cultural community which it has pleaded for, and I think specifically of the Disney report, for five years? Why not now when they support this being done?

Madam Speaker, on the contrary, there is a broad consensus among the cultural groups in this country which shows that they have every confidence in the Applebaum-Hebert process which is quite different from the process initiated by the previous government. It so happens that our formula, namely, to hold in-depth consultations with the arts and culture sector in all areas of the country, is preferable by far to the process initiated by the previous government.
However, having initiated this process and established a commission consisting of outstanding Canadians from all areas of arts and culture in this country, I feel that before making or proposing any changes, we should have a chance to see what general orientation the commission would like to see this country take in the cultural sector.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It was alluded to previously that the Minister of Finance will be meeting with his colleagues this weekend to discuss economic conditions in the country. Energy Administration Act

The House resumed from Thursday, April 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-103, to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to continue my remarks on Bill C-103. Since the adjournment of the House last evening some interesting information has come to my attention, and that is that this bill is adding additional taxes on existing taxes and increasing inflation. Today the CPI in the United States has dropped for the first time since 1965; their first quarter inflation rate is now down to 1.5 per cent.
The bill we are discussing, Mr. Speaker, is adding fuel to the fires of inflation. It is not solving the problem this country is suffering from. Our inflation rate is going up because of government expenditures and taxes, but the United States is now down to an inflation rate of 1.5 per cent in the first quarter. I think this government is incompetent and doing a great deal of damage to this country, and I am going to continue to discuss this bill which I think is a disaster for Canada.
This bill is like so many programs this government has introduced which benefit incompetent operators and force the competent and highly skilled people to move out of the country. The November 12 budget is an extension of Liberal thinking. I am relating this to Bill C-103 because it results from the 1980 budget. I am relating this to the oil industry because that industry is suffering from lack of funds. Because of this lack of funds there is no incentive to invest in Canada.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on November 12 removed interest deductibility. He will make the argument that he is still permitting an amount up to $10,000 and people with immense investments are able to write off their total investment. But I am talking about the guts of Canada, middle Canada, the ones who take the risk. I am talking about the $18 billion I referred to last night which left Canada. That was risk money. Not only has the government removed the wealth from Canada, but it is now removing the guts from the middle of Canada, the people who are the risk takers. They are the people who had the courage in the past to believe in this country. This bill is doing the same thing again. It is discouraging people from investing.
Through this National Energy Program the government will tax savings in the life insurance industry. This money in the insurance industry is a large sum. In the past a proportion of it was invested in the Canadian west, but the government is going to tax it. All this government does is tax, tax and tax. This government has one tax laid upon another. Why does this
government not get some creative programs together rather than taxing the guts out of this country?
What amazes me the most about this government is how its backbenchers always stand up and vote for every piece of legislation. If their leader stands up, they all stand up. However, in this energy legislation that we are dealing with, a peculiar situation has cropped up. It affects every member from the province of Quebec and they should consider it when they vote on this bill. I am talking about the expropriation factor.
I have had the opportunity to discuss the problem with people from Mirabel. Those people had 80,000 acres of land expropriated. They have no one on that side who will listen to them; therefore, they are now coming to me. On Thursday, April 8, some of these people came to Ottawa to talk to the minister who was supposed to be here. He told them that he would be in the House at 12:15 p.m. to meet them. He was not there. Their own Member of Parliament avoided these people all day. Eventually, my office located where their member was which enabled them to present a down payment to buy back the land.
I say to members on the other side that by voting for this bill, under which the province will have no approval regarding expropriation, they are hurting everyone in the province of Quebec. Let me tell hon. members on the other side, having dealt with those fine gentlemen from Mirabel-those poor people whose lands were expropriated, taxed for the right to be expropriated and who have not been given a chance to buy back the land-they are the ones they will be hurting and they are mad. I understand why people are not voting Liberal in the province of Quebec. It is very simple; they are not being represented. I am pointing this out to hon. members because the name of any member who votes for this bill will go to that association at Mirabel from my office. I have a responsibility to those people and the reason I have a responsibility is the same responsibility I had for the people whose land was expropriated at Pickering. At least they had a fighter, and I am going to fight hard on behalf of these people. If the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) were here, I would really attack him on this point.
I am delighted to see that President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) here today. We are talking about economic incentives in Bill C-103. The President of the Treasury Board wrote a book and in his book he talked about economic incentives. It was a sound book and a good book. It was the kind of book that could have been written by somebody on this side, but the President of the Treasury Board is an expert in his field.
On March 26, 1982, the President of the Treasury Board spoke to the Calgary Chamber of Commerce. I do not believe he wrote this speech himself; I believe it was written for him by the bureaucracy. In his speech he mentioned that one of the reasons he entered political life was because of his frustration with the bureaucracy. I have to endorse that stand because it is the reason that brought me here, too, and I acknowledge that.

April 23, 1982
In his speech he said "It is not necessary for the government to be involved in commercial business enterprises." If that is the case, how can the President of the Treasury Board vote for Bill C-103, vote for Petro-Canada and vote for the creation of more Crown corporations that always lose money? I do not know how the President of the Treasury Board can say one thing in one place and say another thing in another. In his speech we find this sentence:
Creation of wealth is what the private sector does best: redistribution of wealth through public sector expenditures and social programs is what the government
does best.
That is a non sequitur. He is saying, "You can do it, and we will take it all away". Will the President of the Treasury Board please explain what he means? I believe his basic philosophy is being destroyed by this government. Further on in his speech, the President of the Treasury Board said this:
-1 believe that government should not displace private capital in business enterprises-
Why should you not give tax incentives instead of funding the way the government does and the way it buys corporations? The President of the Treasury Board also said that he believed in supporting investment activities. Why then is the President of the Treasury Board against interest deductibility? The President of the Treasury Board also said this in his speech in Calgary:
Canada has high interest rates because we have high inflation.
As I said at the beginning of my speech, the CPI in the United States has gone down for the first time since 1965; it is now at the rate of 1.5 per cent. There is no logic to the President of the Treasury Board's statement, and I hope he will answer all of my questions.
Toward the end of his speech he said something that really upset me. He said:
-that the government is in business suggests to me a necessary corollary of equal importance: that of bringing business and businessmen into government and the policy-making process.
The business and the business community were not brought into Bill C-103. The people out west are destroyed. The investors in Canada have been hurt. But the ones who have been hurt the most by this energy program are the small entrepreneurs. The government's energy policy has destroyed the man who is the long-haul trucker, the service contractor, the flat-rig operators and indirectly the automobile industry, because for every job lost in the west two jobs are lost in Ontario and Quebec. But that is what the government is recommending. Would the President of the Treasury Board please put forth his own ideology and quit mimicking the ideology of his emperor?
This government works on half programs. A good way to describe Bill C-103 is half a U.S. program and half a U.S.S.R. program. The half I refer to of the United States would be the windfall profits tax. The government has to tax something so that it is not inequitable to society. But the U.S.S.R. half is the tax to be imposed for Canadian content, to nationalize the oil industry in Canada. The Liberals may call this the Canadian
Energy Administration Act
monetarist's dream, but the rest of Canada call it the Canadian monetarist's nightmare.
I have close contact with my constituents. I hear from them constantly. They know that I am in here Fighting. They know the tough situation with which I am faced. They know that backbenchers opposite are like a flock of sheep who vote on all bills even though they do not believe in them, and this is true even for some of the cabinet ministers. The Liberal government is like a barn full of hogs stampeding to the trough. Every piece of legislation is the same-grab, grab, grab, take it away.
The government, through the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), provides band-aids. Let us talk about these government band-aids. For example, there is the summer employment program. In good times it is of great benefit to assist students in obtaining jobs, but this year the program is setting up daycare camps for the children of the unemployed. The unemployed have nothing else to do. I believe this is morally wrong because it breaks up the family unit. The government should try to hold families together. This is what Canada is about. In the last 14 years the Canadian family has fallen apart, the individual family has fallen apart. The minister gives a band-aid solution to create labour. It is taken away with Bill C-103 and given through another program. This is wrong.
I should like to review a few of the financial implications of Bill C-103 and how it is hurting people. We must keep in mind that every job lost in the west affects two jobs in the rest of Canada. For example, the net internal funds generated by Imperial Oil stayed flat between 1979 and 1982, but I should like to point out that taxes imposed during the same period- and some of these taxes have been imposed but not legalized- have gone from $1,254 billion to $2,712 billion. This comes very close to a 200 per cent increase in two years. This is what is happening. The government is grabbing it all, leaving little money for the little guy, not providing any funds for large multinationals, and taking away incentive for multinationals to find new oil in Canada. Instead the government implements a compensation charge which amounts to 24 cents per gallon out of the pockets of Canadians to subsidize the multinationals to purchase overseas products and to export $6 billion worth of jobs every year.
I draw the attention of hon. members opposite to an article entitled "The Energy Crisis is Over" which appeared in the November, 1981, edition of Harper's magazine. They should read this article concerning the American energy crisis. Although it is old right now, it is holding true even more now than it did when it was written. Why is the energy crisis over in the United States? It is because President Reagan expanded the philosophy of Mr. Carter, which was a basic belief in private enterprise, and removed all controls on oil. The leftwing media jumped on this and said, "Disaster, this is disgraceful; it will push up the price of fuel 10 or 12 cents." I do not need to say any more, but by May of 1981, prices had

Energy Administration Act
started to fall; with private development the prices started to fall in the United States. Bill C-103 is the absolute reverse and hurts the country. It is destroying initiative in the private sector and the possibility of self-sufficiency. It is doing absolutely nothing for the country other than filling the grab bag of the Liberal government.
Who are the real losers in the legislation? It is not the government. It will be the government in the long run, but today it does not realize this. When that much money is taken out of society, who are the real losers? The real losers are middle Canadians or working Canadians who are the guts of the country. I should like to relate the situation in Canada to the figures in the United States where there are lower taxes, lower CPI and lower inflation. Canadians will pay higher taxes with this bill. Also it is creating higher unemployment, higher inflation and higher rates of interest. As I mentioned last night, higher interest rates were created by the deployment of risk capital to other countries. Bill C-103 will certainly Canadianize the oil industry in the United States and drive it out of Canada.
Who will be the beneficiaries of this legislation beyond the government? It will be foreign banks and passive Canadian investors who put all their money in safe Canadian bonds. Canadians should really consider the safety of those bonds. We have great potential and assets behind us, but we are not doing anything with them. We are not producing. I have challenged the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley). I think he is an honourable gentleman who is trying his best, but what is the government doing to create productivity in the country? It brings in Bill C-103 which removes people from the employment ranks in the west and in this part of the country.
I should like to continue on this point by referring to something which I was told this morning. On April 2 I referred to an engineering company connected with Lasco Steel, a very successful corporation which was moving its offices from Whitby. I obtained the facts of the matter this morning, that this was a direct result of Bill C-103. A senior officer of the company told me that its personnel was reduced by 50 per cent since the introduction of the National Energy Program. It has dropped from 323 people to 151 people, which is actually more than 50 per cent. On April 2 I also indicated that the engineering firm was moving its office to Texas or perhaps that it was closing its office. It is not closing its office in Whitby, for the sake of clarification, but nine senior engineers are being moved to Texas. These are nine qualified Canadian engineers. The Minister of Employment and Immigration referred to the fact that his department has to bring in 20,000 to 25,000 skilled people. I believe this is so because many people are being driven out of the country. This gentleman told me, "Yes, it is true that we are cutting back seriously. We hope it is over and that we will not have to lay off any more employees, but any future expansion will take place out of the country". Also he referred to the fact that over the last 12 months the firm had been hoping that something would be resolved on the Alsands
project. The Alsands project is the tragedy of Canadian industry, the tragedy of the Ontario economy.
Also I should like to refer to the fact that Ferco Engineering put together a consortium of six engineering firms called Tars which guaranteed one million man hours of work. He wants to know what will happen because his company cannot keep people employed. He does not know how it will keep them involved. What the government is doing is having disastrous and tragic effects.
I would like to illustrate how a few other industries are affected by Bill C-103; for instance, the rubber industry. Contracts for the manufacture of hundreds of millions of feet of conveyer belts have been cancelled or delayed prohibiting further expansion of the rubber industry. Fewer car tires are being produced because all our cars are being imported with the tires already on them. The government does not demand Canadian content wherein we could ship rubber tires abroad for those cars which are to be imported.
Steel works and rolling mills are being affected. I have already mentioned Lasco Steel. That company is now down to 40 per cent of capacity and it is one of the most successful Canadian steel companies. The manner in which they must operate now is to employ their workers for one week in every three. The reason for this is that they cannot afford to carry the inventory while we have high interest rates.
Another company which I contacted indicated that it had 402 tons, involving 1,500 man-years, lost. It has been dislocated because they have been forced to lay people off. The National Energy Program and Bill C-103, instead of trying to deal with problems which may arise in the future, is just attempting to grab money now without any concern for the future.
I will not dwell on the problems of the automobile industry.
Another sector which is concerned about Bill C-103 is the wire, rope and cloth industry. Just imagine the potential millions of yards of wire rope that is not being produced. We should be proud of the fact that this is a competitive Canadian industry which produced an excellent finished product in Canada.
Another industry adversely affected by this bill is the structural steel industry. Algoma was ready to sign a contract with an engineering firm in order to expand its operations and thereby employ more people in northern Ontario, which is a critical part of Canada. But this bill has forced the postpon-ment of those plans. Algoma is in a holding position, as is the rest of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I represent the Algoma constituency and just this morning I talked to the president of Algoma Steel. He told me that indeed it was spending $240 million this year on the expansion of its tube mill. As well, it plans to spend over $1 billion in the next five years on the expansion of its facilities.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) raised that point. I agree that Algoma is planning to spend that amount of money. I acknowledge that Algoma is preparing for this expansion in anticipation of proceeding, but I gave this example in relationship to the fact that Algoma was in a hold position, the same as Canada is in a hold position. The hon. member should check with Algoma and its consulting engineers.
The hon. member referred to the fabricated pipe industry and said that he thought it will proceed. The provisions of Bill C-103 will make certain that it will not proceed. The compensation charge encourages the importation of oil into Canada, the export of $6 billion a year and that Canadian oil is not used or developed.
We can also look at what has happened to the boiler and pressure vessel business. That industry has almost shut down. I am sure that my colleague, the member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer), can confirm this fact. He is faced with the prospect of his constituents who work in the boiler industry being unemployed. Once again it is a result of Bill C-103, which proposes to take money from the private sector and transfer it to the government trough. It is unfair and inequitable.
I am sure everyone knows what has happened to the valve manufacturers. Fortunately, since the tariff is not excessively high in this area, that industry is not able to export their product to the United States. However, some of the U.S. concerns have been told of the undesirability of importing so much from Canada. Since there is no demand, valve manufacturers cannot sell their goods in Canada. As a result, workers have been laid off with the anticipation of more severe lay-offs in the future.
The turbine manufacturers and the pump industry have also reassessed the situation. Their conclusion from reading Bill C-103 is to ask what prospect there is for success when the government takes away all hope from Canadians. Contracts for the manufacture of compressors have been cancelled virtually every day in the last year. There is no longer any compressor industry-which was a major industry-in this country.
One of my constituents is the director of the electrical association in my riding. He wanted me to tell the government what Bill C-103 is doing to the companies in his association. It is removing the incentive to expand. He told me that they had a number of contracts from the west which are now being
Energy Administration Act
cancelled. People in Ontario are hurting, with the exception of those people represented by the hon. member from Ottawa because his area is well protected by the civil service. There is no industry on which he has to depend. I invite him to come to my riding and talk to some of my constituents.
I could go on and cite examples of other industries in trouble, such as the transportation equipment industry. Trucks and semi-trailers which were being built to be sold in western Canada were being partially constructed in Ontario and shipped to western Canada. I can cite one example after another.
I would like to read some conclusions about the National Energy Program made by the C.D. Howe Institute. I am sure the hon. gentleman this institute was named after would be shocked and embarrassed to see what his Liberal successors are doing. The conclusion by the institute states:
The NEP is an economic policy that is severely constrained by political factors. It represents the federal view of how Canada's energy resources can be used as a tool to orchestrate the country's economic future, with the federal government conducting and playing the leading role.
It went on to say that Ottawa has failed to realize that it is a co-operative arrangement between the provinces. The leader of the Liberal Party has stated that there must be co-operation with the west for this program to succeed. The institute went on to say:
But the policy takes risks. If the attractiveness of competing activity in the United States has been underestimated, if reduction in oil demand has been overestimated, if the oil sands projects are delayed much longer, and if the response to frontier options is weak, Canadians may pay lower prices and own more of their industry by mid-decade, but they should also be aware that part of the price may be lineups at the gas pumps.
I am speaking in this debate on Bill C-103 because I am concerned for my children and my grandchildren. We have stopped development in Canada. We have encouraged multinationals to buy oil overseas. We have done everything to discourage the private sector of this country.
I hear the President of the Treasury Board and I do know that his philosophy was right before he became a cabinet minister in this government. I admired that gentleman; I have read his book. However, will he get his guts together and his back up and stand up for Canada and for the people he represented for so many years as a very able lawyer in Montreal?
Hear, hear!

I also appeal to the hon. members of this government who are from Quebec to please consider what has happened and go to talk to the people at Mirabel who have been ill treated before endorsing unilateral expropriation under this bill. I ask them to go and talk to their people to see how they have suffered.
Therefore, I say that this bill will mean nothing but another disaster to Canada. I plead with the minister, withdraw it. We took 16 days in which to try to get our point across. I guess the

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-103, to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak once again on another item in the continuing saga of the national energy policy. This one is particularly insidious and is very onerous to the Canadian people because it will take a lot of money out of their pockets. If we look at the principles behind the national energy policy which are again incorporated into Bill C-103, we find that what the government wants to do is to impose strict control on the Canadian oil, gas and energy industries. The government wants to be able to direct where energy will come from, how it will be sold, the prices at which it will be sold and the amount of public revenues which will be generated. The government wants to regulate and tighten all aspects of the Canadian energy industry.
The members of the NDP may be a little more honest than the hon. gentlemen opposite. Their policy is to nationalize the energy industries and they are quite frank about it. They want to nationalize the oil and gas industry in the same manner they want to nationalize the steel industry, the banking industry and everything else. Pretty soon they will want to nationalize the little family farm which is presently somewhere down on the list, but its turn will come.
The hon. gentlemen opposite have a different approach to things. They are a little bit more intelligent, and I give them credit for that. They are a little bit more clever. I am not saying much, because one does not have to be too clever to be more clever than the average member of the New Democratic Party. The plan of the Liberals is to turn the energy industry into a utility where people will be able to make a certain return on investment, but there will be no real incentive to go out into the market and compete or to try to find new sources of energy as cheaply as possible, because the profit motive will no longer be there. Energy in Canada will be produced on a utility basis. The investor-owned corporations still involved in the industry, if they survive, instead of trying to maximize their profits and efficiency, consider new ideas and take new risks, will try to justify as large a cost base as possible under the new system in the same manner as many people in the gas distribution business at the present time. This is really the aim of the government. A few senior bureaucrats in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources will be able to control all energy matters in Canada by diktat.
That is really what the national energy policy and Bill C-103 are all about. The government has a plan to control, not necessarily own, the Canadian oil and gas industry and other
April 23, 1982

aspects of the energy system. It is not really necessary to own things in order to control them. The government envisages Petro-Canada as having much greater participation in the business than we would like on this side, but at this point in time it does not see it as encompassing the entire industry. The government found that it could control the industry without necessarily owning it or nationalizing all of it, although we have seen from the bills put before us in the last couple of weeks that it does intend radically to increase the nationalization which has been going on for some time.
I think that such a system as envisaged by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and his cabinet colleagues will be detrimental to Canada in the long run. I have some concern as they are taking over a dinosaur. They are using billions of the taxpayers' dollars to take over an industry which has reached its peak. I think that funds would be better invested, if they were to be invested by the public sector at all, on new and upcoming sources of energy. Instead of buying out the oil industry which is at or past its peak, the government should be devoting the same taxpayers' dollars to investments which will return a greater dividend in the years to come.
The policies being pursued by the government will result in higher prices in the long run. They will result in decreased efficiency of the energy industries because the incentives will no longer be there. The utilities in the business will operate on a bureaucratic basis very similar to that of government. One can see that at the present time there is very little difference between the way in which the bureaucracy of Imperial Oil operates and the way in which the bureaucracy of the government operates. There does remain one fundamental difference in that the bureaucrats, for want of a better word, who work for Imperial Oil can get fired if they screw things up too badly, whereas people in the employ of the government rarely suffer that fate. However, there is a general tendency on the part of the technocrats in the Liberal government to want to extend their existence and the way they do things to Canada in general.
I think it is important that we maintain a proper distinction between what properly comes within the purview of the government and what properly should come within the purview of the private sector of the economy. It is my opinion that the energy industries in Canada can best be developed by the private sector.
We are slipping into state control of the basic resources of the country. The analogy I like to think of is the ancient hydraulic civilizations of Egypt and Mesopotamia. The governments of the day controlled all life in those earlier civilizations by controlling the most important and basic resource, water. If the state controlled the water, they controlled everything. They had control over the individual lives of all the people. They controlled everything through control of the major resource, water.
Energy Administration Act
I am sure the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others in government are thinking in exactly the same terms for Canada. If they can control energy supplies, they can control everything.
It is frightening when you think about it and where a country like Canada, which heretofore has had very high regard for the freedom of its population, might end up. Look at what might result from these policies that have been consistently employed by a Liberal government for some 14 years.
The other aspect of Bill C-103 is revenue. The Government of Canada has discovered in the oil and gas business a new source of revenue. I should not say new because there have always been reasonable taxes on oil and gas at the federal and provincial levels in the past. It now looks upon energy, oil and gas in particular, in the same way we look upon whisky. It costs a couple of dollars to produce a bottle of whisky and there is $8 or $9 tax on it. The tax is out of all proportion to the value of the commodity. This may be well and good in the case of a luxury such as alcoholic beverages. We can live with that and accept it. Most people are quite prepared to pay very high taxes on alcohol and tobacco because they are strict luxuries. We do not really need them. Hopefully some of those moneys will go to use in other areas.
People do not mind paying high taxes in those areas. However, the Liberal government has adopted that way of looking at taxation on oil and gas. Unfortunately, people have become used to it. When they go to the gas pump, of every dollar they pay, 30 cents goes to the explorers, producers, refiners, distributors, marketers, retailers, wholesalers and everyone else in the business doing production work. The remaining 70 cents goes to governments, federal and provincial. People are accepting that. It is wrong that they have been led into that acceptance. When you go to the gas pump, the price per gallon or litre should specify the amount of taxes you are obliged to pay to various levels of government.
We should not treat gasoline, and especially home-heating oil, the same as whisky. Taxes and royalties on energy products should bear a reasonable relationship to the true value of those products. A rate of royalties and taxation not dissimilar from the federal sales tax would be reasonable. I am surprised the Canadian public has accepted what is going on. I guess there has been some kicking back; unfortunately, their protestations have been in vain. Those opposite have pursued them relentlessly, beaten down the Canadian public and forced them to pay these energy taxes.
This bill legitimizes the 28-cent a gallon tax that has been unlawfully collected for some time, in some instances going back two years. Canadians know those taxes were unlawful, that there had been no parliamentary approval given. What could they do about it? They could not go to court. They would have spent millions of dollars on a lawsuit to prove they had been unjustly taxed and a few weeks later the government would have turned around and brought in retroactive legislation, such as it is now doing. That is not the way taxes are

April 23, 1982
Energy Administration Act
supposed to be levied in a free country. It is not the way citizens of a free country should be subjected to a government that has very little else in mind except getting as much money as possible by bleeding dry the taxpayers of the country.
Remember the mandate given to the present government in the election two years ago; remember the election slogans at that time-"Vote Liberal and keep energy prices down". The 18-cent a gallon tax that had been proposed by the then minister of finance was shot down across the country. Now what do we have? We have a tax of about 70 cents a gallon. That has been in the increase in the price of a gallon of gasoline since those characters opposite found their way back into office as a result of promises to keep gasoline prices low.
The national energy policy in Bill C-103 has been sold to the Canadian public on three bases. The government said it would Canadianize the oil and gas industry. It said this would result in energy security and in fair prices. The National Energy Program and Bill C-103 fall down on all of these. Canadiani-zation was in progress and would have continued. The excessive rate of Canadianization, especially through nationalization and ownership by government and not by individual Canadian citizens, has had an adverse effect on the level of our currency. It has chased foreign capital out of the country at a time when it is most needed. That was not done in a balanced way.
We have had example after example presented to this House of the ways in which the oil industry and capital have been chased out of this country. The rigs are leaving the country as well as technical expertise. People in the industry have been leaving the country. I do not want to recite this time and time again. I just want to bring it to the attention of the House once more. May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext: Order, please. When the House rose at one o'clock the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) had the floor.
Hear, hear!

If I recall correctly, Mr. Speaker, before the lunch break we were discussing the follies of the Liberal Party and in particular the failures of the Liberal cabinet when it came to formulating a reasonable energy tax policy. These, unfortunately, are subjects with which many Canadians are very familiar. We were describing how the national energy policy and its tax implications have driven out capital, equipment and people from Canada. By virtue of the National Energy Program, the Alsands project and the Cold Lake project, which would have done so much for the areas in the west in which they are located and for industries right across
Canada from coast to coast, have been set back and likely delayed indefinitely. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) gave a vivid description showing how these policies would affect many manufacturers in his constituency, everything from the rubber industry to valve manufacturers.
If we look at the supposed energy security aspect of the NEP, we find that this also has failed. Canada is just as dependent today, if not more so, on imports of oil from Mexico and from Saudi Arabia as it was before the implementation of this ill-founded policy. If we look at the fair prices component of this supposed policy, we see that this has not worked either. There is still disparity between one region of the country and another with respect to oil and gas and energy prices. There has been a tremendous increase in prices. We have not got security, we have not got fair prices; what we have got is higher and higher taxes, and higher taxes again under Bill C-103 which we are dealing.
The three enumerated aspects of the policy put forward by the sales pitch the government gave us-the Canadianization, the energy security, and the fair prices-have not worked.
What the national energy policy really entails is an increase in federal control, an increase in centralization. That is what they are really after. And it means also an increase in taxation. Look at the billions of dollars that are going to roll into federal coffers as a result of taxation measures associated with the national energy policy. There will be $50 billion alone as a result of the agreement between the federal government and the province of Alberta. That was the expected amount; the government has already made plans to spend that money. Now, because of the glut of world oil and the lowering of prices, their financial estimates are likely to be away out of line, resulting in even greater federal government deficits. That will lead again to inflation and to a continuation of the sorry state into which the Liberal government has allowed the Canadian economy to fall.
I have dealt with the overall policies contained in Bill C-103, and at this time I would like to go through the bill and deal with it clause by clause. I do not want to deal with the policy matters so much as with the specifics of the bill.
No. That is for committee.

The first item we notice is a change of name. It used to be the Petroleum Administration Act. The Petroleum Administration Act was originally brought in for a very specific purpose at a time where there had been a rapid escalation in the price of OPEC oil. It was felt necessary to shield Canadians from what was expected to be a short-term fluctuation in oil prices. That is how the government sneaked it through the House of Commons in the first place. Unfortunately, it is now becoming a permanent fixture. It will be in the statute books of Canada forever, and it no longer deals just with petroleum. The name is changed to the Energy Administration Act. That is what it will now be called, and if we look
April 23, 1982

through the bill we find that it also deals with coal and coal products. We wonder where the government will go from there. Does the government want to control uranium and geothermal energy? Where will it stop? The idea in this bill- and the government has now made it known-is that it is not just a temporary thing to deal with petroleum but a statute with which the federal government will control all aspects of energy in Canada for ever and ever. We will never get rid of this thing.
Let me deal with the oil export charge. Many of the observations we could make about this particular aspect could equally be made about the other provisions in the bill. The oil export charge was originally $8 a barrel. Under this legislation it will be raised or authority is given to the minister through order in council to raise the export charge to some $350 per cubic metre. According to my figuring, that comes out to a little over $50 per barrel. We are authorizing a manyfold increase, from $8 to $50 all in one fell swoop. What we are doing is giving authority to the minister and his colleagues in cabinet to increase taxes up to that maximum at any time they want.
Surely Parliament should jealously guard its privilege to set rates of taxation. We should not give blanket permission to the government to increase taxes whenever it wishes. We should make it mandatory that whenever the government wishes to impose additional taxes on the Canadian public it come back and get authority from the representatives of the people of Canada in this House.
We know what happened to Charles I.

1 would like the same kinds of things to happen to some other people in this House with whom we are familiar.
With respect to the way this measure is to be administered, originally there was a board. I think it was called the petroleum administration board and it was charged with the administration of policy. That was something of a safeguard. I am afraid that boards and committees appointed by the Liberal government very often are composed of people who are appointed because of their party affiliations. We all know that, but at least they are outside government. They are people to whom complaints can be made. Presumably they have the time and the competence to look into the administration of affairs and come to judicious decisions not based on the political expediencies of the day. They have not always worked out in the way we would have liked, and I am sure occasionally they have done things at the persuasion of the government-things which people on their own might not have done-but these boards have served a purpose. However, under this bill the various boards which did exist in a safeguard capacity are now to be dispensed with, and it will be the minister, and the minister alone, who will decide how much tax we will have to pay, how much rebate we will get and how all the complex technical details contained in this legislation will be dealt with. There is no safeguard any longer. Previous safeguards were not
Energy Administration Act
as good as we might have wished, but now there are no safeguards whatsoever. The minister and his senior departmental officials will administer every last little item in this legislation, which undoubtedly will be passed into law.
If we look at Clause 10 of Bill C-103, we will see how the power and authority of the minister are being increased. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will end up as a super minister. He will be the reincarnation of C. D. Howe. In fact, C. D. Howe will look like a piker, in view of the power and authority to be granted to one individual super minister. With the powers Parliament has already been forced to grant the minister under Bill C-48, for instance, and other energy bills Parliament has dealt with in the last few weeks, this man and his colleagues will virtually control the whole Canadian energy industry. Nobody else will have a say at all.
The minister will be sloshing around in millions or billions of dollars of taxpayers' money. He will be giving it out here and taking it in there and exercising all kinds of powers and authorities which normally should go through the parliamentary system. However, because these provisions are outside the normal budgetary provisions and the normal way by which we deal with tax matters, and because these funds are isolated from the Blue Book, taken out of the budget and put into special funds about which nobody really will know what is going on, the minister will be in his glory. He will be wallowing around in billions of dollars of taxpayers' money and directing the energy industry from a central location here in Ottawa.
That is the type of situation in which we will find ourselves if this type of legislation is consistently passed by the House of Commons. Time and time again we on this side of the House have pointed out these dangers and, because of the overriding majority of hon. members opposite and the way they stand up and vote whichever way they are told, we are getting ourselves into a sad situation.
Let us look now at the second provision of the bill, the one dealing with transportation fuel and the compensation recovery charge. The effects this tax-for that is what it is-will have on the Canadian shipping industry-for example, the shipping industry on the Great Lakes-have been well described to this House by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). All we have to do is read the editorial pages in technical journals dealing with shipping and the management of seaports to find out what the effect on the Canadian transportation industry will be. Here again we are giving the government blanket authority to raise taxes up to a maximum of $350 per cubic meter. According to my reckoning, that is about $1.60 per gallon. Again we are giving this authority retroactively, in this case back to May 1, 1981.
Another clause of the bill with which I have some difficulty-I just want to mention this in passing because it is a major item, and it has been discussed many times-is Clause 13, which claims Sable Island for Her Majesty in right of Canada. We are all well aware of the dispute between Nova Scotia and the federal government over the ownership of Sable Island. In this bill we do not keep to the good faith presumably shown in

Energy Administration Act
the recent agreement between those two governments; the federal government claims that ownership for itself alone.
Clause 15 of Bill C-103 grants to the governor in council the authority to establish maximum prices for crude oil produced in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, where this government claims sole jurisdiction despite the wishes of the people who live there. This is a battle we fought when Bill C-48 was debated and I do not want to repeat the arguments I made then. However, I would point out that this clause will create a great deal of difficulty in the north. People do not like being governed by regulation out of Ottawa; they would like some form of consultation. They feel they have the same ownership rights as any other part of Canada. They do not feel those resources are exclusively for the benefit of Canada, although they are quite willing to share them.
The government of Ontario retains the right to say what the maximum price should be for oil produced there. I think it should be set by market conditions, but the jurisdictional authority lies with the government of Ontario, the same as in Saskatchewan or Alberta.
However, this bill indicates that the federal government is going to grab for itself alone the authority to make those decisions in the two territories. The people who live there pose the very sensible question: Why should we pay the highest price in Canada for oil and gas when the federal government sets our wellhead price and does not attempt to equalize the price between the southern areas and the northern territories where much of Canada's oil and gas will be produced in the future? This bill would be another opportunity to legislate some form of energy revenue-sharing agreement between the territories and the federal government, as has recently been done with Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. But it is another opportunity lost.
The Government of Canada is selling out the interests of northerners in order to be able to supply southerners with a slightly reduced cost of energy for a short period, thereby keeping themselves in office. I suspect that is the real reason. It seems to me grossly unfair that oil and gas produced in the north is to be sold in the south for less than the people in the northern producing areas have to pay.
Another objectionable part of the bill is Clause 18, which deals with penalties for non-payment of these taxes. Under the old legislation, for a summary conviction the penalty was $20,000 or six months in jail. Under this legislation the fine can be $100,000 and one year in jail, or five times the fine and twice the jail sentence. Under the old legislation, for a conviction by way of indictment the maximum penalty was two years in jail. Under this legislation you will be liable to a fine of $1 million and/or five years in jail. I think these penalties are vicious, cruel and unusual punishment. It seems that in this country people get off kind of lightly for many Criminal Code offences, but if you forget to pay your taxes then the government comes down hard on you with these penalties.
The same argument I used in the case of oil in the Northwest Territories applies equally to this bill's provisions concerning the pricing of domestic gas. The federal government will have the authority unilaterally to set gas prices in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. However, the provinces will come in for some of the same treatment here. They are going to find out what it is like to be ruled by Ottawa. There is a provision in there which provides that if, in the opinion of the governor in council-which really means the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in this case-the federal and provincial gas pricing agreement is deemed to be ineffective, then the federal government by order in council has the authority to regulate those prices.
That is a terrible thing in a country where we would like to see agreement between the federal and provincial authority. Surely it would be to everyone's advantage to have some measure of co-operation between the two levels of government. But here the Liberal government says "No, if we do not like your suggestions on gas pricing then we will do it ourselves; we are not going to take any notice of the provinces. If we do not like what you have to say, we have the authority to do exactly what we want." That, Mr. Speaker, is what the government gives to itself in this bill.
In the former legislation the section dealing with domestic gas prices had a built-in safeguard. If the federal government set gas prices in a province it had to file that information before Parliament within a certain time, and there had to be the opportunity for debate because this is a very unusual use of the federal government's powers. Parliament would then have the opportunity to rescind it by way of a vote, which is unlikely to happen with a majority government but at least it made Parliament cognizant of the fact that this was a major and unusual use of federal powers. In Bill C-103 that safeguard has been taken away. The government can set gas prices and they do not have to tell Parliament about it. The safe containers legislation is an example of how the government misused its authority in that it failed to bring before Parliament certain statutory instruments issued under that legislation.
Let us go now to the petroleum compensation charge. Originally in Bill C-94, the omnibus bill, that dog's breakfast we eventually got rid of by ringing the bells for two weeks, the charge was to be a maximum of $20 a barrel. I guess we can claim a victory for Parliament because under the new legislation the maximum allowed by way of governor in council authority, the way government can raise taxes, has been reduced from $20 a barrel to $12 a barrel. This is something of an accomplishment for Parliament, in my opinion. But we must remember that under this one charge authority is to be granted for an increase in taxes in the amount of 35 cents a gallon, which is still a significant increase.
Again, under Section 30, the board which administered the petroleum compensation charge in the disposition of funds raised by way of that authority has now been eliminated. Once more, the authority lies solely at the discretion of the minister.
