The minister enjoys the prerogative of levying this charge and determining its amount, saying where that money will be spent and who will be granted the proceeds.
One of the worst things that has happened as a result of the petroleum compensation charge is that now refiners have found it cheaper to use imported oil than to use oil produced in Canada itself. This is an anomaly. I suppose no one could foresee this when this complex legislation was brought into effect in the first place. But so much for the designs of the national energy policy where encouragement is given to refiners by virtue of tax relief to bring in oil from Mexico, Saudi Arabia and other countries and not to use oil produced in Canada but to leave it shut in. This does nothing for Canada's balance of payments. It is an anomaly and I hope it can be rectified in the near future.
I notice that the provisions of the petroleum compensation charge which originally dealt only with petroleum, as in the title, is now being extended to coal products. If someone finds a good way to produce synthetic crude from coal, they will not be able to enjoy the benefits of that discovery because all the benefits will be taxed away. All the benefits will be taxed away the minute anyone uses initiative and expertise to come up with a better process advantageous to Canadians to reduce our dependence on foreign oil and to reduce our balance of payments. People will not be able to enjoy the benefits because the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will come along and take any profit which might be made from the discovery by way of taxes.
Next I want to deal with the Canadian ownership charge. Under Bill C-94 the amount would be a maximum of $4 a barrel. Again, Parliament can claim a victory by having reduced that amount to a maximum of $1.15 a barrel, or thereabouts if you work out the numbers of dollars per cubic metre. It is still under 3.5 cents a gallon. Another little charge is tacked on there somewhere else. The Canadian ownership charge is a misnomer for the Petro-Canada tax. It is a tax levied at every gas pump in the country to help pay for the government's acquisition of Petrofina. It amounts to something well over $1 billion Canadian. This amount is proving very useful for alleviating unemployment in Belgium, but it is not doing very much at all for Canada.
That matter has been debated many times in this House, and I do not wish to be repetitive and go over the whole Petro-Canada issue again. However, I do like people to be aware that every time they go to a gas pump they are paying a few cents a gallon toward the acquisition of Petrofina. This money would have been better used in looking for new gas and oil and energy resources within Canada.
The special compensation charge in the bill could amount to 5 cents a gallon if the government uses all the taxing authority which is to be made available to it under this bill. What we can say about the special compensation charge is that it was absolutely unnecessary in the first place. It was arrived at because of the inability of the federal government to agree with the government of Alberta over oil pricing. The deal that was worked out by December, 1979, was set aside and it took
Energy Administration Act
two years of fighting and bickering before an agreement was reached. The Canadian people, those who buy gasoline at the pumps and who use oil and gas to heat their homes, have paid for this failure on the part of the government. Canadians have paid for the antagonistic attitude the federal government maintained during those years.
Once more, the authorities previously invested in the petroleum compensation board have been transferred to the minister and his departmental officials. Again protection has gone.
One of these days I would like to make a list of all charges- the compensation charge, the special compensation charge, the ownership charge etc. There are so many of them floating around that never show up in the blue books. People do not know the extent of the taxes they are paying. The only thing they know is that a considerable amount of tax is paid when ever they buy gasoline at the pump.
Of all the energy bills originally comprised in Bill C-94, Bill C-103 is probably the worst and the most insidious. It certainly has the greatest impact on Canadians through their pocket-books. It will take money from every Canadian in this country. If we are at all concerned with the onerous levels of taxation in Canada, especially on energy, and if we are at all concerned with the methods of taxation and the way in which taxes should be imposed and seemed to be imposed by the people's representatives, then, Mr. Speaker, I submit that we must vote against Bill C-103.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to address a few words to Bill C-103, which will amend the Petroleum Administration Act and set up the energy administration act. This is a very important aspect of the National Energy Program. It has a number of elements to it. They relate to the oil export charge provisions; the establishment of the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge; amendments to the domestic oil and gas provisions; amendments to the petroleum compensation charge and petroleum compensation provisions; the establishment of the Canadian ownership special charge and it gives authority for the Canadian ownership account; finally, there are provisions relating to the special compensation charge.
Today I would like to talk about the Canadian oil industry as it was before the introduction of the National Energy Program in the fall of 1980. I want to talk especially about the dominance by foreign-owned oil companies and how the Canadianization program under the NEP is being implemented under this particular program.
Toward the end of 1980 we, as Canadians, were faced with an oil and gas industry that was very heavily foreign owned and controlled. A full 72 per cent of oil and gas revenues ultimately accrued to foreigners. Furthermore, some 78 per cent of these revenues were accounted for by foreign-controlled companies in Canada. This compares with levels of foreign ownership and control in the United Kingdom of some 52 per cent, and some 10 per cent to 15 per cent in the United States.

April 23, 1982
Energy Administration Act
I think we must put the matter in perspective. We hear Americans complaining about the move by the government to Canadianize the oil and gas industry. We must ask ourselves, if their oil and gas industry was 72 per cent controlled by foreigners, rather than 10 per cent or 15 per cent, what would be their attitude, response or concerns, especially with the prospects over the long haul of oil and gas reserves increasing dramatically in value as they have done in the last seven or eight years? Over this period of time there has been an increase from $2 or $3 per barrel to some $40 per barrel. The long-term forecast suggests that this will probably continue. We must think about the additional revenues which will flow out of the country in terms of interest and dividends.
Not only was the level of foreign ownership and control very high, but a glance at major industry competitors clearly shows the dominance of foreign companies in the Canadian oil industry. Eleven of the 15 oil and gas producers were foreign owned and controlled, with the top eight positions being held by foreign companies. Not only was the domination by foreign companies pervasive, but it seems likely that the situation will become even worse. Future major oil supplies in Canada will not be from traditional sources in the western basin. Rather, oil and gas supplies will be increasingly derived from massive oil sands plants on exploration sites in the Arctic Islands and on the east coast offshore. These future sources of supply require vast sums of money and a great deal of technology, technology which is often beyond the financial resources of small Canadian-owned independent companies. Foreign-owned companies were and in many cases still are in the best position to take advantage of the future opportunities of oil and gas reserves.
Given this situation, the following questions must be asked. What government in the developed world would tolerate this degree of foreign participation in an industry as significant as oil and gas? What government would allow such dominance in a strategic industry which in Canada's case is responsible for 10 per cent of our gross national product? These were the types of questions which the Canadian government faced in relation to its own economy in the autumn of 1980. Its response was the Canadianization objective and the policies embodied in the National Energy Program of October 28, 1980. In the NEP we sought to establish greater Canadian control of the oil and gas industry by the establishment of, and the increase in control by, Petro-Canada, as well as by the establishment of the Canadian ownership account which is embodied in this bill.
In the year since the announcement of the National Energy Program, some strides have been made toward Canadianization. The eighth, Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, the fourteenth, Aquitaine, and the eighteenth, Petrofina, largest oil and gas companies have switched from foreign ownership to Canadian ownership and control. The level of Canadian ownership measured by upstream production reserve revenues have increased by over 6 per cent as a result of some $7.5 billion in
mostly private sector acquisitions. Petro-Canada, the nationally-owned oil company, now has refining and marketing facilities across Canada, after its recent acquisition of Petrofina.
Although the government is generally pleased with its progress, it realizes that there is much to be done. Before the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation this week it was rather impressive when the representatives of Petro-Canada indicated that for the $2.9 billion of investment made by the Government of Canada in Petro-Canada, the market value of the company is now estimated at $8 billion to $9 billion.
Of course, this is a nice increase in the value of that asset and an impressive capital gain. It is important for taxpayers to see a capital gain of that magnitude. If we look at the entire oil and gas industry and at the amount of capital gain we will see during the course of this decade, there is no question that we will see even greater gains than this one, which represents almost a 300 per cent increase. If we calculate the dividends and interest payments which will be made to foreign countries, principally to the United States, we see the urgency of getting on with the Canadianization program. It is for this reason that we are proposing the establishment of the Canadian ownership charge and the Canadian ownership account.
The Canadian ownership special charges, used initially to help Petro-Canada's acquisition of Petrofina Canada Incorporated, will consist of the following: a special charge on domestic petroleum received for processing or consumption in Canada and foreign petroleum amd petroleum products imported into Canada. Currently the charge is $7.25 per cubic metre, which is the ceiling set by this bill for the charge. No further increases are authorized by this legislation. Second, there will be special taxes increasing the natural gas and gas liquids tax, which is a tax on marketable natural gas, propane, ethane and butane. Increases in the natural gas tax are now 14 cents per gigajoule. The increases in the taxes on propane, ethane and butane are $3.55, $2.60 and $3.95 per cubic metre respectively. These amounts are the ceilings set in the bill for the increases. They would not be applied to exports of natural gas and gas liquids. No further increases are authorized by Bill C-103.
Revenue from these charges will be placed in the Canadian ownership account. Initially the revenues will be used to help defray the cost of the Petro-Canada acquisition. In future, the use of any funds from the Canadian ownership account for other acquisitions would have to be authorized by the governor in council, acting on the recommendation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Such uses would be subject to a negative resolution in Parliament, in the Senate and the House of Commons.
It should be made clear that the direction of the Canadianization thrust has also been toward the mobilization of predominantly private Canadian investment-from existing companies, pension plans, insurance funds and individuals. To a great extent this policy has succeeded, since all but one of a dozen acquisitions to date have been by private companies. Furthermore, the government is acting as a catalyst for the
April 23, 1982

establishment of a co-operative energy corporation which will bring into the oil and gas sector the savings of millions of Canadian co-operative members. Senator Argue played an important part in negotiating that arrangement with the Canadian co-operative movement.
A misconception which we have heard, particularly from abroad, is that the government is creating an unattractive environment for foreign firms which will reduce the value of these firms, thus allowing them to be purchased at fire sale prices. This is simply not true. The facts are that Canadian companies have paid prices which are above market value for foreign-owned assets. Furthermore, foreign-owned oil and gas subsidiaries trading in Canadian exchanges have done no worse than their Canadian-owned counterparts.
Another misconception involves the belief that the Canadi-anization policies for the energy sector will be applied in all energy sectors of the economy, specifically the minerals sector. The government has already stated that this is not the case and the evidence on the difference in the foreign ownership and control situation in the two industries is a major reason for the difference in the policies.
Finally, the objective of Canadianization does not mean that foreign investment and ownership in the oil and gas business is no longer wanted in Canada. Canada is well known for its exciting geological potential. The combined financial and fiscal incentive package offered by the government makes Canada one of the most attractive countries for investment. For example, a foreign investor operating in the north will, after tax deductions and incentive payments, be spending only 53 cents of every exploration dollar. In fact, a recent comparison made by Petro-Canada of rates of return expected by a foreign investor from a representative pool of new oil shows the following: Canada lands, 27.7 per cent; 24.4 per cent in the United Kingdom; in the United States, 21.6 per cent; and in Norway it is 18.3 per cent. I repeat that these calculations are for foreign investors.
The figures reveal that we have created an environment which will be attractive to foreign investors when compared to other locations. The government welcomes their participation and asks only that they take into account the legitimate aspirations of Canadians to own a share of this vital sector of our economy and exercise some control over decision-making in the petroleum industry.
This view is widely supported by the vast majority of Canadians. Indeed, it is one of the most popular programs established by the government in the National Energy Program. The results of a poll conducted by the Canadian Petroleum Association last year show that 84 per cent of Canadians favour the government's move to make the oil and gas industry at least 50 per cent Canadian-owned by 1990. This is a very important statistic because it is taken from a poll which was carried out by the Canadian Petroleum Association. Many of its senior members are not Canadian-owned petroleum corporations.
Energy Administration Act
With respect to the Canadian ownership special charge, I would like to mention the signficant change that was made to these provisions as they appeared in Bill C-94. The legislative authority that appeared in Bill C-94 to raise the Canadian ownership special charge above the present level has been removed. Under the new amendments, the existing Canadianization charge can be decreased, but not increased beyond that level by order in council. The change is as follows: the ceiling on the Canadian ownership special charge on petroleum has been lowered from $25 to $7.25 per cubic metre. The ceiling on increases to the excise tax on natural gas has been lowered from 60 cents to 14 cents per gigajoule and the ceiling on increases to the excise tax on natural gas and gas liquids has been lowered from $17 per cubic metre to $2.60, $3.55 and $3.95 on ethane, propane and butane respectively.
Therefore, this bill which is before us today comprises an important part of the National Energy Program. It puts in place the amended price which was foreseen when the policy was adopted; that is, that we would have one price for the oil in the existing western basin which was produced at relatively lower cost and that we have a higher price for the much more expensively produced oils discovered in the high Arctic or on the offshores of the east coast or the Beaufort Sea. We would have a new oil price for the tar sands, for tertiary recovery, as well as for the discovery of new oil in the western basin.
It also provides for the compensation on imported oil which has allowed Canadian oil prices to be well below world prices wherein we have had a gradual build-up in prices during the last several years. Consequently, we have had a greater growth than many western industrialized nations.
Therefore, I would contribute my support for this Energy Administration Act which is before the House. I hope that it will receive the full consultation, discussion and detailed consideration which has already been given to the Petro-Canada bill in the standing committee. At this point, I must compliment the members of that committee who have been meeting from nine o'clock in the morning until ten o'clock at night with only a break at lunch and dinner. I can attest to the fact that the committee is working very hard. It will have a great deal more work to do in the next few weeks in considering the bills which are before us. However, I am sure we will carry it through and conduct a thorough study at the committee stage on all bills, but particularly on Bill C-103 which is one of the most important aspects of the entire National Energy Program.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to contribute to the debate on Bill C-103. This bill is an act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and a measure to impose many new taxes on Canadians. This bill authorizes two taxes which are already imposed upon energy consumers. Certainly, it bears almost no resemblance to the promises which were made by the Liberal Party during the last election when they promised Canadians cheap gas.
The petroleum compensation charge is currently levied at $6.30 per barrel. This results in price increases at the pump of 24 cents per gallon. The Liberal candidate who ran against me

Energy Administration Act
in the last federal election stated that gas would not go up any more than 8 cents to 10 cents per gallon under a Liberal government. Obviously, he was being provided with false information by the Liberal Party with regard to cheap gas. But what is new about that? In addition, the PCC provides that the maximum would be about $12 a barrel and could thus raise prices by about 24 cents.
The Canadian ownership charge which was used to pay for Petro-Canada's purchase of Petrofina is levied at $1.15 a barrel and results in gasoline prices being 4 cents per gallon more expensive. As was pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), all that money-approximately $1 billion-went to Belgium in order to buy this company and provided absolutely nothing for the Canadian economy or any Canadian.
The government earns a total of approximately 60 cents per gallon of gasoline. A sampling of some major United States and Canadian cities has shown that the price of gasoline in some U.S. cities is less expensive. For example, the price of gasoline in Seattle is almost 3 cents per litre, or 13 cents per gallon, less than that sold in Vancouver. The price of gasoline in Detroit and Windsor is virtually the same. Other regions in the United States sell gasoline at 99 cents a gallon. Of course, this has been brought about by government regulations being removed. However, in Canada we see more government regulations and interference which drives the price of energy higher.
The government has given various assurances that the price of Canadian oil will remain below prevailing world prices. The price of old oil will not exceed 75 per cent of average world oil, and the price of new oil will not exceed 100 per cent on a floating year average. However, this does not protect consumers as the bulk of the federal taxes are added after the comparison is made. Thus, while crude oil may be cheaper at the wellhead, consumers may actually be paying more than the world price at the pump. This policy of the Liberal Party to pay world price for oil has had disastrous consequences on the price of gas and heating oil and what have you. This actually goes back to about 1960 when the Diefenbaker government introduced the road to resources program to open up the north. But unfortunately, in 1963, the Liberals dumped the road to resources program and did absolutely nothing about developing our resources in the north. If they had continued with Mr. Diefenbaker's road to resources program we would be selfsufficient today and we would not be paying world price for oil.
Also, imports are much higher than needed to complement Canadian supply. Canadian crude is being shut in. The result is that the PCC is being used to pay for imported oil that we do not even need.
The Conservative Party has long maintained that the introduction of these two taxes by notice of Ways and Means was improper. Now the multiple injuries arising from the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) are still being assessed. This budget is a far cry from the sensible
April 23, 1982
budget brought in under the Progressive Conservatives, as theirs was not a budget which was trying to look for every conceivable, possible way to tax Canadians more and more. There is certainly a sharp contrast between the two.
Now, along comes the Liberal energy minister's National Energy Program, riddled with bullet holes which he tries to plug with all the dexterity of a one-armed paper hanger. The actions he announced last Thursday, designed to adjust his programs to the new reality of world oil glut and the shutdown of production in western Canada, managed to offend both producers and consumers in equal measure. Will these patch-up measures introduced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) result in resumed production in Canada's oil fields and the accelerated programs of exploration which the minister foresees? I ask, will they do that? The answer, almost certainly, is no. The minister himself indicated he knows it when he said that if the people who buy and sell oil do not act as he urges them, he will implement further measures if warranted. They will be warranted, all right, especially if the world glut continues and world prices keep coming down, as the minister hopes and prays they will not.
I would like to speak for a few moments about the bell ringing and about our reference for having the bill split up. We now find that the 98 cents a gallon taxing authority sought by the minister has been reduced to 52 cents a gallon. The bell ringing has saved Canadians 46 cents a gallon in possible taxes under Bill C-103. On April 4, the Conservatives voted against the 53 cents a gallon tax. The Liberals voted for the 52 cents a gallon tax. One should compare that to 18 cents a gallon tax.
Because the bill was split, this tax will be voted on three more times in the House of Commons between now and June 30. It can be stopped or reduced if the Liberal MPs can be convinced to vote against it. Concerned Canadians should write or phone their Liberal MPs and ask them to vote against the 52 cents a gallon taxing authority, as they promised in the last election that gas would not be increased over 18 cents a gallon. Public support for our bell ringing has already saved 46 cents a gallon. So let us see the Liberal hon. members getting down to business here and stopping this other huge increase.
Bill C-102, which is tied in with Bill C-103, would allow cabinet, not the elected members, to set up unlimited numbers of Crown corporations. There are 438 Crown corporations now. We do not need any more Crown corporations. Taxpayers will pay but the people they elect will not be able to vote on whether or not the taxpayer wants cabinet to run around spending money on new businesses. There will be a tax of four cents a gallon forever, to allow cabinet members to buy whatever they choose.
Bill C-101, which is also connected with Bill C-103, would allow the Liberal cabinet to give $4.9 billion of taxpayers' money to the board of directors of Petro-Canada to spend as it sees fit. The Liberals voted to decrease money for health care and post-secondary education by over $500 million. Instead, they want that money to go to the board of directors of Petro-Canada. So much for their priorities.
April 23, 1982

We all remember Bill C-94, an earlier energy bill, and Bill C-103 is a devilish offspring of Bill C-94. The Liberal government has conceded that the energy bill will be split into eight separate bills in ways suggested by the Progressive Conservative Party. In addition, the Conservatives forced the government to concede to a timetable which guarantees over three months of debate and guarantees Canadian citizens the right to come before committees. It also guarantees members of Parliament the right to vote a minimum of 24 times on the separate parts of this package. It guarantees MPs the right to move amendments and have them voted on.
It is the Canadian people who achieved a victory which will now allow taxi drivers, homeowners, farmers and small businessmen the right to come before a Parliamentary committee to explain to Members of Parliament how a 98 cents a gallon tax increase will affect the cost of food, clothing and shelter. Then Canadians will have an opportunity to judge their Members of Parliament on how they will vote on that massive tax increase.
A few things to remember about Bill C-103 and the other energy bills are that they amend 15 current pieces of legislation, they create four new taxes, they allow the government to form new energy companies at will, they include 28 cents of taxes on each gallon of gasoline, and they provide for increases of another possible 70 cents. I will certainly be using these figures in the next federal election on the campaign trail to indicate clearly to the electorate that they will not be able to believe anything they hear from any Liberal after what the Liberals said in the 1980 election. At that time, they said they would lower interest rates and would give Canadians cheap gas. They will not get away with their packaged lies in the next federal election.
The bill incorporates many parts of the National Energy Program, which has been opposed by the Conservative Party from the outset. The Conservatives were voted out of power because of an increase of 18 cents a gallon for gasoline. The Liberals have already raised gasoline prices by about 65 to 75 cents a gallon, and now they plan this further increase of 75 cents a gallon in this series of energy bills. The Trudeau government's concessions to split the omnibus energy security measure into eight separate bills to be examined by a special standing committee able to call witnesses and to assign ample time for meaningful debate in the House of Commons and at committee is exactly what the Conservative opposition requested, beginning last December. So we finally won out in that battle. The concession that a special standing committee will deal with all aspects of the energy legislation over a six week period is something we requested more than a year ago. The assigned time will effectively mean that the House of Commons will spend most of April debating second reading of various bills, that there will be six weeks of special standing committee examination with witnesses, and that most of June will be devoted to report and third reading debates in the House of Commons. The Conservative Party has brought that about.
Energy Administration Act
Let me just comment on gasoline and heating oil prices. There have been 15 increases in the price of petroleum since the Liberals came into power on a promise of keeping prices down. The 1980 summary showed the last increase in 1980 brought total increases for that year to $4.70 west of the Ottawa Valley and $4.88 a barrel for eastern Canada. The Liberals promised that increases would not exceed $4 for the year. They also promised that gasoline prices would rise by no more than 14 cents a gallon. My opponents said eight cents to ten cents. Others across the country were saying 14 cents. They could not get their act together on what they were not going to give the Canadian people. In fact, increases in many centres across Canada approach twice this amount.
The 1981 summary shows that prices of gasoline rose by about 12.5 cents per litre or 56 cents a gallon, and heating oil by 7.9 cents per litre or 36 cents per gallon during the year. The Conservative Party stated we would not raise the price of heating oil. The last thing that should be increased in this country is the price of heating oil. However, that does not bother the Liberals.
In all, crude oil rose in price by $8.40 a barrel, not including special levies of $1.86 imposed and subsequently removed during the year. Federal taxes accounted for 75 per cent of this increase. In comparison, the Conservative budget would have raised crude oil prices by $4.50 a barrel. You can see the difference.
I now want to deal with oil sands. The blame for the delays with the oil sands projects, both Cold Lake and Alsands, rests squarely on the federal government. If the government had been reasonable with Alberta two years ago, both projects would have long been underway. The immediate problem with Alsands is beyond the government's control. World prices are falling. That is not the time to negotiate a rate of return.
The government's Canadianization policy is a distraction from the real task of finding oil. Since the mid-1970s, Canadianization of the oil and gas industry had been proceeding at a measured but accelerating pace. The Canadianization policy, a bastardization of the policy that we introduced while in power in order to differentiate ours from the Liberal's nationalization policy, has completely destablized the industry.
The government has completely twisted the rationale behind high energy costs. Whereas our government was prepared to accelerate the rise in the price of energy in order to encourage new supplies and only secondarily to encourage conservation and raise government revenues, the present government has raised prices, first, as a means of increasing government taxes, second to conserve oil and only third to encourage production.
While consumer prices for gasoline are only slightly more than they would have been under the Crosbie budget, heating oil is much more costly. There is no equivalent to our energy tax credit which Canadians would have been enjoying these past two years. They have lost that. The consumer is worse off under the disastrous budget of this Minister of Finance.

April 23, 1982
Energy Administration Act
The larger Canadian companies have used the Canadianiza-tion incentives as a means of growing to a point where their debt load threatens their existence. They have not found any more oil as a result of their increased size, but now they can at least compete with the multinationals.
Small Canadian-owned companies have experienced the brunt of the National Energy Program's contradictory policies. The pricing and exploration policy has more than removed any benefits from Canadianization. Some of the multinational oil companies have chosen to sell out, but most have had no choice but to stay with a decreased exploration budget. They are laying off large numbers of employees at the present time.
In conclusion I will say that two years of this Liberal government has produced an increased burden on consumers and a certainty that Canada's chance at obtaining oil self-sufficency by the early 1990s has been lost forever.
The way to measure whether you have a good government, good policies or good legislation is by the investment you attract. Not one aspect of the National Energy Program or of Bill C-103 has attracted one dime of investment. The NEP was responsible for driving over $18 billion of investment money out of this country. That was the last nail in the coffin. The NEP has just about destroyed the free enterprise system in Canada. This country cannot survive economically with that amount of money leaving the country.
The New Democratic Party has spent considerable time goading the Liberal government into these nationalization policies. They will have to accept a large part of the responsibility for the implementation of the National Energy Program, Bill C-103 and all the other bills with regard to their disastrous effect on the Canadian economy. It is certainly helping economic policies in the United States. They would be a lot worse off there if it were not for our $ 18 billion.
Now that the NEP has got the Liberals into this disastrous nationalization policy, their leader and the premier of the province of Manitoba have called for exchange controls. Their answer to the disastrous NEP is to bring in exchange controls. When you ask for such controls to be brought in to stop the outflow of capital from Canada to the United States and other countries, you do not have an answer to anything.
If you have good government and good policies, you attract money rather than drive it out. I hope the Liberal Party will wake up and realize that it is doing absolutely nothing to attract investment and to assist the Canadian economy. If they had any sense, they would withdraw this whole energy package and start again from scratch. I advise them to get free enterprisers to assist them, those with a knowledge of the industry, rather than socialist academics who write reams of theory on these different policies. We on this side can certainly lend them some people to draft sensible policies with regard to energy. I suggest they take another look at the Crosbie budget. It would be a step in the right direction.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are dealing with an extremely complex piece of legislation. When
it is sorted out and implemented, we will have gone a long way toward helping this country progress and participate in the great future that will be ours. It should be in place before long. Like many Canadians, I abhor the fact that every time action legislation is planned, there is a long time lag before it is implemented, due to tactics that serve no purpose other than to obstruct.
Before talking about the petroleum compensation charge and a few other items, I should refer to the interesting outlook of members opposite about the energy program in Canada. On the one hand they want the private sector to look after it all. They make interesting observations about our energy program, but they do not get their act together. A predecessor of mine, who has been mentioned in the House in two different ways by members opposite, the Hon. C. D. Howe, was responsible for helping Canada, particularly in the west, to get their product to market by pipeline. That helped to raise Canada to a new plateau and helped with our GNP. It provided revenue from outside sources through the marketing process and by bringing the opportunity to the manufacturing centre to obtain energy from an exciting new source in quantity large enough to be significant.
What we are about to do now through the National Energy Program, I believe, is another of the very important items in the building blocks of Canada. We must recognize that the country and the world is changing profoundly and changing quickly in recent years. We have had the opportunity to be flexible and do better than most countries partly because of our natural resources but more because the will of the people is to make this country work and to take advantage of our resources, share them with one another and take a responsible position in the world in which we live.
At present there is a lack of activity in the oil industry, which is having a profound economic effect, for many reasons. It seems to be a temporary situation. I honestly believe that when this bill has been passed, when a total national energy program is in place, we will have opportunities for Canadians to control their own resources, and that is of fundamental importance to the good of Canada. We will see Canadians participating in the development of the oil and gas industry as never before and reaping the profits from it. The people of Canada will more properly have their say on how the resource-which by everyone's admission is a non-renewable resource and is not infinite-will be husbanded for the future use of the country. We can make immense use of this prime energy resource at this time in history and at the same time reduce our dependence on other parts of the world. That is a key element of the National Energy Program and the legislation before us. It will put us in a position where we will not have to rely on decisons made outside our country. We can make those independent Canadian decisions that are not hidebound to what happens in the area south of us or in Europe or in the Arab states.
April 23, 1982

We want to maintain control over our destiny, we want to be able to plan our future in our own Canadian way. In order to do that, some things are absolutely essential. One of the essential elements is the opportunity to control that nonrenewable resource, oil and gas and subsidiary products.
It is not only for its fuel and heating capabilities but for all of the other chemical elements that we count on oil to produce, to drive the economy and to give us a chance to trade in the world on a truly competitive basis. We will be able to make many of the rules ourselves here and will not have to depend on other people and on their resources. No other country would allow a great percentage of its prime resources to be controlled by others. The National Energy Program gives us an opportunity to regain control of our resources and put them to good use.
The process has been an interesting one. It is not admitted that there has been as much consultation as really has taken place in this area. The opposition is trying to create the impression that no one on this side of the House ever listens, that we on this side never sit down with those involved in the industry and learn from them.
At another point in my life, Mr. Speaker, I was involved very much in a body interested in the business community, namely, the chamber of commerce. I still have some private enterprise thoughts and feelings and the desire to ensure that the government listens to all segments of Canada, including the business community, particularly in things of this nature. A great deal of consultation has gone on and continues to go on.
What the hon. members opposite fail to say is that one of the big opportunities of the National Energy Program is that Canadians will be encouraged to invest in Canada and that by doing so we will gain from our investment in our own resources.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
We must recognize that we really need to have Canadians with a very strong sense of being Canadians, in position in large enterprises such as the oil and gas industry. We must have such Canadians in place so that they view things from a "Canada first" point of view. If members opposite find that a disagreeable or socialistic attitude, I am sorry. I am a proud Canadian. I feel we have the right to expect that we as Canadians will benefit most from our resources. As a trading nation we must have the investment dollars coming from other parts of the world. We must keep our doors open wide to that. The National Energy Program does not destroy that idea. It simply means that Canadians will be encouraged and will be given greater incentives to take a larger share of their future and be in a better position to direct their future.
I heard some interesting comments during this debate. Some hon. members spoke as if the National Energy Program were the cause of all our economic woes. There has to be some recognition that the current glut of oil was not anticipated.
Energy Administration Act
That may be the prime reason for the lack of activity in such projects as the Alsands project.
We all know we must keep searching for new oil. The petrochemical industry will be a large part of our present and future energy for the next 30 or 40 years. All of a sudden we have a downturn in our economy and in the world economy. There are other parts of the National Energy Program which have already begun to work. Conservation is beginning to have its effect. We find that we now have a glut of the product. We find we do not have the same sense of immediate urgency to look for those petroleum resources that we know are there.
We should look into this aspect of it. We know that part of the ongoing future of Canada will be in the megaprojects. One of the most important megaprojects will centre around the tar sands of Alberta and the resources of other parts of Canada as they come onstream. We have been blessed by the fact that it appears that we have more conventional sources of petroleum available to us than we expected. Those resources still exist and we must not forget that. We should realize the potential of the Alsands and other such resources. Nevertheless, the need to do so is not as immediate as it once was.
A timing dilemma was thrust upon us by a very sudden change in the world situation but, being the eternal optimist, I do not think we should be fooled by that because I expect we will see a greater need for energy in the future as the world's economy and Canada's economy turn around. The wisdom of putting in place a National Energy Program with which we can all live will be seen.
I for one am glad we now have a limit on the time for debate of the important matters before us because we really need to put into place legislation on which people can count for a period of time, and when the National Energy Program is passed and implemented, those people who will want to invest in this field-and many of them will be Canadians-will have a feeling of certainty. They will have the necessary knowledge of how to proceed and where to proceed.
However, the bottom line is that the National Energy Program will give us energy self sufficiency on schedule. It will give us the proper amount of Canadian control, and it will give Canadians the opportunity to invest more heavily in their own country and to benefit to the maximum from their prime energy resource of the day coming from petroleum.
I am pleased to have had this chance to participate briefly in this debate today. I hope we will continue to act in the proper fashion and get this legislation through so that we can carry on.
Finally, I remind all hon. members that there has been a great deal of consultation with the producing provinces and the people in the industry. They have been listened to, and I believe we have come up with the game plan Canada needs and can live with, and I believe it will help us to enjoy the prosperity which rightfully belongs to us.

April 23, 1982
Energy Administration Act

Mr. Speaker, before beginning my principal comments I would like to refer to some of the remarks which have been made by the two previous speakers on the other side of the House.
I find it quite distressing that there should be such a broad difference of opinion on the course this country should follow in energy matters. We seem to have a dialogue of the deaf. Perhaps it is a dialogue of the deaf, the blind and the mute. I do not know how the mute carry on a dialogue, but there seems to be no understanding whatsoever-there is a disbelief-that the National Energy Program as set down in the House in October of 1980 has so far succeeded in driving Canadian enterprise out of this country. The minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) just does not believe that. I do not know why he does not believe that because it has. Somehow he has managed to convince the "trained donkeys" behind him of his view of the degree to which that false budget, which was more properly called the "National Energy Program, of October of 1980" has, in effect, destroyed a great part of the industry in Canada.
I heard expressions of hope from the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters). We must exist only on hope. We cannot survive on the basis of the legislation which is being brought before us. All we have left is hope.
This legislation basically boils down to the question of Canadian ownership. I think that is the main thrust. But I wonder if it is. When the Liberal Party says "Canadian" and "Canadian ownership", it somehow feels that ownership through the government is the same thing as Canadian ownership. Perhaps that is our problem. 1 do not believe that. I believe that Canadian ownership is ownership by Canadians individually, not through their government. Hon. members opposite have talked themselves into believing that when they say "Canada" and "Canadians" they are the spokesmen for Canadians. On a majority basis they are spokesmen here, I agree, but let hon. members opposite not carry this to the point where when they say "Canadian ownership" they mean ownership by the Canadian government. That is what they intend to do through Crown corporations.
Earlier this week we dealt with one of the eight energy bills which is designed to authorize the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to create as many Crown corporations in the energy field as he wishes. Presumably that will Canadianize something. It will not; it will "governmentalize", it will nationalize, but it will not encourage Canadians to invest in the energy field. We are being required to invest in Canadian enterprise through the tax system.
When the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) spoke, he said Canadian ownership could be encouraged by providing an investment climate in Canada which would induce Canadians to invest in this country. I do not believe this bill will create that kind of climate. I suppose there is a basic difference in philosophy between hon. members opposite and hon. members on this side of the House-this side to a certain point only, excluding the NDP.
The example of White Farm Equipment Company comes to my mind. White Farm Equipment Company was operating in Canada, and it got into difficulties. As a result of an application by the parent company-I think it was a 49-51 per cent proposition, the 49 per cent still being held by the parent company in Texas or somewhere in the United States-FIRA authorized the American parent to take over the White Farm Equipment Company of Canada, which manufactures not just trucks but farm implements as well. Why would an American company take on a bankrupt Canadian company? I think the answer is pretty obvious. The investment climate for Canadians to invest in Canadian companies is not nearly as good as the investment climate in Canada for Americans to invest in Canadian enterprise. That is the whole problem, and hon. members opposite consider that they are "Canadianizing" our petroleum enterprise when, in fact, they are destroying the incentive for Canadians to invest in their own country.
I have mentioned it before, and I will mention it again: whatever surpluses I have to invest I invest in Canada, and I have run into some pretty serious losses in the last couple of years as a result of the policies of this government.
That is why you are so bitter personally.

I am not bitter. I am proud to have invested in Canada, but the decision to do so has been mine. That investment was not made through taxation. That is where the crazy notions come in. Why should we be required to invest in things that they choose? Why should I not have that freedom of choice? That is where the philosophical difference is, and it is high time the Canadian people realized it. In Liberal eyes Canadian ownership means government ownership; in the eyes of the Progressive Conservative Party it is ownership by Canadians through individual decisions.
I was speaking of taxes. We are having trouble in the extracting industries, as I think the hon. member for Algoma and the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon would be aware. However, there is one extracting industry which is flourishing, that is the Department of National Revenue, the greatest extracting industry in Canada. It extracts more money from Canadians now than it has ever done in the past, in order to create what this government claims to be a Canadianization policy. A governmentalization policy is the best name for it because that is what it is.
If it were not so disastrous and distressing one would have to admire the ingenuity with which this government's public servants can devise means of sopping up through taxation every single pool of potential investment in Canada and discouraging individual investment decisions. It is destroying the Canadian ethos. I think of my mother and father who decided before the turn of the century to head west, one from Ontario and one from Nova Scotia. I still think of that trip in about 1890 when they went by train from Truro, I guess it was-because I am sure it did not stop at Stewiacke-to High Bluff, Manitoba. They went by their own decision to open up
April 23, 1982

this country, and how many are doing that today? Unfortunately, not too many.
The public servants 1 mentioned, who are so intent on sopping up everthing they can by way of taxes, are motivated of course by one thing, the high burden of debt this country is faced with, which was created by that side over the past 13 or 14 years. We celebrated 14 years of debt earlier this week. They are also motivated, I suggest, by the principle of socialism, in total disregard of the experience anyone can see with their eyes half open. It is beyond the doubt of any reasonable person that governments are not fitted to run industry as efficiently as the private sector which has other motivations. The comfortable security of state employment is enough to deaden initiative and incentive for all time, and it causes the public interest to be disregarded in an enterprise-oriented role.
Public servants have a role to play, I do not question that. It is a matter of service to the public. But they are not, by training or the nature of their jobs, capable of making the same sort of decisions about running an enterprise that the private sector is.
How about Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson and a few others?

The public service by its nature and makeup is just not equipped to be entrepreneurial, particularly when management is loaded with political appointees. And I can think of a lot of them. That role properly belongs to the private sector.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I have not been over-dramatizing the situation. But, unfortunately, the drama and tragedy of Canada is there for all to see. This government, in its economic, constitutional and other policies, seems bent on destroying this country, for reasons which I am at a loss to understand. It is sad to have to make that comment but I am forced to because, as I look back over just the last nine and a half years in which I have been in the House, I have seen Canada's unity, its potential being, shattered and lying there in front of us.
Last Saturday should have been a day of rejoicing, and it was because the Queen was here. It was not a day of rejoicing, let us be honest, because the Constitution was here. I think everyone, if they are honest with themselves, is prepared to admit that. I was delighted the Queen was here, but what changes did she bring with the Constitution? It should have been a day of rejoicing, but that feeling is tempered by the problems created by this government through its confrontational approach to every problem, economic, linguistic or others, and this in a federal union. It is not only nonsense, it is disastrous, sad and disgraceful.
On Wednesday of this week, Mr. Speaker, we gave second reading to a bill which would permit Canadian corporations to expropriate from non-Canadians, and which entitles them to apply for and obtain special concessions from the federal government such as write-offs, subsidies, loans and licences, which would be denied to those corporations who do not meet the requirements of Canadian ownership. I listened to that debate on Wednesday and heard some members on the other
Energy Administration Act
side say this will encourage foreign investment. That, Mr. Speaker, defies human logic. Why should any non-Canadian risk his money in an enterprise in Canada when he is faced with, not the likelihood or the possibility, but the certainty of having that investment taken away from him without any say in it whatsoever? I cannot imagine anything more calculated to destroy the desire of foreign investors to invest in this country. And these trained donkeys over there all voted for it.
Well, we are not horses' asses like you are.

As I have said, I cannot imagine any non-Canadian investing in Canada with such a provision on the statute books. If non-Canadian investment is being deliberately discouraged, from what source is the investment to come? That was not a very smart comment the hon. member just made, was it?
I would not have said it if it were not true.

We have heard there is no sufficient private investment in Canada to fill the void. I have asked myself for a number of years since being in the House, and for a number of years before that, whether there has been any real encouragement to Canadians to invest in Canada. The fiscal climate is just not geared that way. It is geared to collect money from Canadians so that the Canadian government can do the investing for them. That is what this government calls Canadianization. But I do not. I do not think that is Canadian-ization at all. I think it is governmentalization, and that is wrong. It is a dead end. There is no light at the end of that tunnel at all.
Stemming from the fact that there is no proper encouragement for Canadians to invest in this country, there are two possible conclusions confronting us. Perhaps the government is planning to bleed Canadians through taxes so that it, the government, can do all our investing for us. That is, of course, a form of state socialism, so dear to the NDP but foreign to the real Canadian Liberalism of Laurier and St. Laurent. I do not understand how Liberalism came on such sad days. If that is not the explanation, is the government planning to drive foreign capital out of the country entirely and leave us as a resource rich country, which is not going to be developed, for some non-Canadian predatory power? Those are pretty extreme conclusions to have to reach. We could become the battleground of the latter half of the twentieth century for those who want the resources we have, which we have so badly abused, and which we have failed to encourage Canadians to reap and harvest.
What sort of real full-blooded Canadianism is this? It is not my vision of Canada, nor, as I suggested in my comments a little earlier, was it the vision of my mother and father when they went out west. Where has Canada's individual initiative gone? I suggest that it is being sapped by this government's attempts, very successful I have to admit, to cause citizens to look to government for all things; womb to tomb, if you like. It

April 23, 1982
Energy Administration Act
is the great Robin Hood. The Liberals are robbing and they are a bunch of hoods, there is no doubt about that. But it is not the Robin Hood of history in any proper sense.
The government has created a brand of Canadians who seem to think that whenever they are in distress or have a little problem they have to rely on government. The government has encouraged that and thereby it has robbed Canadians of their initiative. Is this being done deliberately? Do not ask me. Is it malicious, or is it just downright stupidity? I wonder if it is MacEachenomics? It could be. One thing certain is that Canada is being taxed out of its patrimony. Canada will end up without its patrimony. I wonder what sort of country it will be when that happens.
A few other elements of our problem need to be underlined. There was a time when Canadians were taxed legally by parliamentary decision. That used to happen. In this bill, as we shall discover, we are being asked to cede-and no doubt the donkeys will assemble in sufficient numbers to grant the cession-
That is not right.

It was the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who used the language. We are being asked to cede to the minister of energy in conjunction with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) the decision on how taxes will be levied.
My recollection of the constitutional history of this institution, in which fortunately we can still speak freely, is that there were a number of monarchs or heads of state who decided to levy taxes on their own without consulting Parliament. In fact, it was that proclivity on the part of a number of British monarchs which brought this institution into being to be sure there were constraints placed on the monarch, that he would act within those constraints and that Parliament would determine what they were, would vote the money to the monarch and he could then do what he wanted.
Now we are seeing a reversal of that. I do hope, Mr. Speaker-because you will be out of a job-that this does not mean the end of Parliament. What we are doing is giving two ministers the power to increase taxes, and that is wrong. This bill also will make legal what has been collected illegally for over two years. The retroactive elements of this bill are really quite impressive. I do not know whether the people in the gallery are aware that they have been paying taxes for which there is no legal statute to entitle the government to collect those taxes, but they are paying them nonetheless. So am I, so is everyone here and so is every Canadian paying them, not only at the gas pump but when paying for fuel oil for furnaces. These taxes have been imposed for over two years. They will now, if this bill passes, become legal.
Finally, the unit that was once taxed-and I think this is supposed to introduce an element of confusion, and it does- namely, the $8 a barrel is now to become taxed on the cubic metre. I still have not worked out just how many barrels there are in a cubic metre or vice versa, but I gather there are more barrels than cubic metres than vice versa.

It is 0.1637? I had better make a note of that because I will need it one day if we go into this business. But the tax limit on a barrel which was $8 will become $350 on the cubic metre. Let us not get too excited about that because it means the tax level will be about $55, up from $8. That is only eight times more than the current tax. I guess we need not worry too much.
May I call it four o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It being four o'clock, the House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's Order Paper, namely, notices of motions, public bills, private bills.

Miss Pauline Jewett (New Westminster-Coquitlam)
That, in the opinion of this House, a full parliamentary review should be undertaken of Canada's external, defence and aid policies to redefine Canada's objectives in these areas.
She said: Mr. Speaker, as you have just said, this motion calls for a full parliamentary review of Canada's external, defence and aid policies in order to redefine Canada's objectives in these areas. Since this motion was first proposed almost two years ago today, there have been several parliamentary reviews in specific areas of foreign and defence policy. There was the parliamentary subcommittee engaged in preparations for the conference on security and co-operation in Europe. There was the parliamentary full committee discussing Canada's relationships with the United States under the NORAD agreement. There was the discussion by the committee of the Canadian Armed Forces Reserves and, of course, the very important task force on north-south relations. There is a more recent committee, which I am glad to say is still sitting, on Canada's relations with Latin America and the Caribbean. Another committee was terminated just a few days ago on security and disarmament in preparation for UNSSOD II. Other committees have also been active in defence and foreign affairs matters, such as Canadian trade relations with the United States. A very important report was made in that regard.
There is no question in my mind that many of these specific parliamentary inquiries have had some influence on government policy, particularly those reports which have forged new paths, developed new concepts, re-examined past practices and proposed different ones. I am thinking particularly of the interim report of the subcommittee on Canada's relations with
April 23, 1982

Latin America and the Caribbean. I am thinking of the full report of the Commons committee on security and disarmament, but of the minority report prepared by six members of the full committee. Also the north-south task force has had some effect upon the position of government in north-south relations. Particularly when the committees, subcommittees and task forces have differentiated themselves from the status quo and have looked at exciting new ways in which policy might be developed, they have been important and influential.
In another respect many of the specific parliamentary inquiries have been valuable because they have brought forth a host of Canadians as witnesses or as brief writers representing hundreds of thousands of Canadians and therefore have helped to increase Canadian interest, concern and involvement in international affairs. Canadians care a great deal that the Parliament of Canada should be involved and make recommendations to the government on these matters. When it looked the other day for a moment as if the Latin American committee would be sabotaged, the protest from the Canadian public was so vast that the committee's life was in fact restored and retained.
We could continue with specific parliamentary inquiries. In the last two years since I put forward this legislation, there have been more than half a dozen. We could have a specific inquiry on the Middle East. Canada's relations there are a very important matter. We could have a specific inquiry on CIDA, its objectives, how well they are being carried out, and whether they should be defined differently. We could have a specific parliamentary inquiry on the structure and operations of the Department of External Affairs. I am sure many of my colleagues and friends in the other parties feel as I do, that we still need a comprehensive parliamentary inquiry to thoroughly examine Canada's role in the world. We have not had a real study of Canadian external policy embracing defence and development policies for approximately a dozen years. A foreign poicy for Canadians came out more that a dozen years ago. Since then there has not been any comprehensive government or parliamentary inquiry.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR REVIEWS OF EXTERNAL, DEFENCE AND AID POLICIES
speechtext: The last one was in 1968.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR REVIEWS OF EXTERNAL, DEFENCE AND AID POLICIES
speechtext:
Yes, the last one was in 1968. Many people such as George Ignatieff, Walter Gordon and others, have suggested a royal commission. Perhaps the matter has reached such a degree of uncertainty about our foreign policy that we should have a royal commission. There are many good things to be said for it, but if we had a parliamentary inquiry with the power to travel across the country and to examine any aspects of Canadian foreign affairs, it might do as well.
There has been no effective leadership from the government in the field of foreign affairs in the last decade. I can think of only one example where Canada played an active leadership role, although it turned out to be only rhetoric, and that is at the United Nations Special Session on Disarmament in 1978 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spelled out his policy of nuclear suffocation. Professor M. J. Tucker said at York
External, Defence and Aid Policies
University in February of this year at a conference on Canada and UNSSOD II:
The strategy itself seemed to hold out hope that something could be done in a tangible way about the nuclear arms race in all its dimensions, while the prime ministerial presence at the special session seemed to suggest that Canada would be actively involved in this process.
Rather than Canada being actively involved in this process, Canada has said and done almost completely contradictory things. The Prime Minister, the Secretary for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) have agreed on one matter. They have said, and indeed even boasted about the fact, that Canada is the only power which could have developed nuclear arms and did not. Canada has now said that it will no longer have nuclear arms on its land and the new fighter aircraft will not be nuclear equipped. They have made a great deal of the fact that Canada has insisted upon there being no nuclear role for Canadian forces in Europe. In other words, they have proudly said time and time again that Canada is non-nuclear. On the other hand, they have found no inconsistency whatsoever in Canada being involved in the creation of the guidance system for the new Cruise missile. It has given substantial grants to Litten Industries, for example, which is helping in the manufacture of the guidance system for the Cruise missile.
More recently, the government says that it has found no inconsistency in Canada's secretly agreeing, as we have now learned, to flight-test the air-launch Cruise missile over Canadian soil.
When we asked the Prime Minister approximately a year ago if he would make any statment on whether or not the neutron bomb should be deployed in Europe, he said that he did not have a position and that it was a matter for the Europeans to decide upon. Not only has Canada contradicted the strategy of nuclear suffocation or its spirit, it has, perhaps even more seriously, contradicted the spirit and, I believe, the letter of its own non-nuclear weapon status.
I cannot understand how the government can state that we are proud of the fact that we will not have nuclear arms on our soil, not equip our forces with nuclear arms or equip our aircraft with nuclear arms but will gladly equip every one else.
I am not the only one who viewed that as illogical reasoning behind its policy. The consultative committee on disarmament, meeting with the ambassador for disarmament, recently shared much the same view.
When a number of Europeans declare that they do not want nuclear weapons on their soil, the government scoffs at them. The government scoffs at the peace movement in Europe and claims that that movement is making unilateral decisions, as if the government itself did not make them. The government scoffs at the Kennedy-Hatfield proposals in the United States, and calls them unilateralist.
The government's position on the nuclear arms position, or lack of position, is so baffling that six of us who are on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National

April 23, 1982
External, Defence and Aid Policies
Defence felt obliged to issue a minority report. Not only does a lack of leadership and follow-through on the part of the Canadian government become apparent in this area, it is evident in many other areas as well. There are some unbelievable contradictions in government policy. Government policy can differ, depending on whether you listen to the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as was evidenced by the Canadian responses to the imposition of martial law in Poland. Its policy with respect to that crisis was vacillating and unpopular.
Another example is Canada's position on El Salvador. Its policy was ill-informed and misjudged. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said on June 17, 1980, at the hearings of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence that:
-Central America is not an area of particular concentration of interest for us.
Last year in the House he said:
-it should be remembered that historically Canada has not had strong or important links with El Salvador. It is a country near our part of the world but hardly a neighbour.
In this same speech given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, he said:
In light of the full circumstances, therefore, as we see them, we are prepared to contest the U.S. policy of military aid but not to protest it; we are prepared to pronounce on it but not to denouce it; we are prepared to criticize it but not to condemn it.
A senior Canadian diplomat abroad reported to me during that period that it was extremely difficult to be a diplomat and had been for some time. The reason for this is that there is no clear foreign policy direction coming from Ottawa with no clear goals and objectives to our foreign policy. There is no leadership within the foreign policy sector in Canada and no leadership displayed by Canada in the international community.
Canada could even have played a role in the Anglo-Argen-tinian dispute, a role which it has often played in the past, that of mediator. I was interested to read in the Toronto Star that Ottawa declined an opportunity to mediate in the crisis and kept quiet about that opportunity. The Toronto Star report, dated April 18, 1982, stated that it emerged from Washington last week, though it went unnoticed and apparently unrecorded, that Ottawa ignored a United States request to help in the mediation. Right at the start of the crisis, according to reports from Washington, U.S. officials had asked Canada to consider how it might serve an intermediary role. Canada apparently refused this request.
Another area where we thought Canada wished to play a creative role involving taking strong diplomatic stands on some occasions and playing the more traditional mediating role on others, concerns the matter of foreign aid and development programs. Aside from the fact that the amount of Canadian aid is less than 0.5 per cent of our gross national product, the quality and direction of aid must be seriously examined. A proposition of our aid which is tied to Canadian goods and services is still too high. Some 80 per cent of all CIDA bilateral dispersements are tied. In other words, 80 per cent of the money spent on bilateral aid never goes overseas. It is spent
here in Canada for Canadian aid to Canadian industry. I admit that Canadian industry does need help during these times, but why is it budgeted as foreign aid? Furthermore, the goods and services provided are often of questionable value to the cultures and economies of developing countries. If these goods and services are useful, they could often be purchased much cheaper from other developing countries.
I could proceed to question the government's policies on the voting of aid funds through multilateral development banks to regimes with the most serious human rights violations. What I want to stress is that the House has never had the opportunity to discuss the terms of reference for CIDA. It is questionable whether or not CIDA has any clear terms of reference regarding development assistance, other than those set by itself or the minister. It needs a very thorough review. This should be embraced in an important aspect of the total parliamentary review which I am requesting and that many of Canada's senior officials in the various departments we are talking about are quietly requesting. This was revealed in Miss McDougall's report.
I will conclude by pleading with other members in the House that in the absence of clear direction from the government in the presence of a multitude of contradictions, some of which I have illustrated, we must have a comprehensive study by a special committee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, which would have the authority to travel throughout Canada and have the time required to conduct a thorough investigation, in order to delineate more effectively where Canada's obligations now lie, what foreign policy interests are vital and what Canada's role in the international community should be.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR REVIEWS OF EXTERNAL, DEFENCE AND AID POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to review some of the current policies which are of importance to Canadians. Some of these issues have been touched, others have not. Canada's foreign policy has been relatively constant. The goals set out in the foreign policy review of 1970 continue to reflect the aspirations of Canadians. Those goals are the fostering of economic growth, safeguarding sovereignty and independence, working for peace and security, promoting social justice, enhancing the quality of life, and ensuring harmonious natural environment. These goals present continuity in Canadian foreign policy.
While the strategies of attaining these goals may change according to the environment, these goals themselves remain unchanged. There must be a constant process of foreign policy adjustment to meet changing conditions in the world, but this does not require an ad hoc, fundamental review from time to time of foreign policy goals or objectives.
Canada's foreign policy has been characterized by promotion of international co-operation and the building of international institutions. We are a middle power, not a major power, and we can only operate by co-operation. This has been the
April 23, 1982

hallmark of Canadian foreign policy since the Second World War.
Canada is dependent on a world of co-operation and openness. The fact is that without this international co-operation and stability, Canada's options for a diversified set of relationships and the ability to conduct a global foreign policy become very narrow, if not so minimal as to be almost non-existent. I would like to deal with some of these current foreign policy issues, and I would say that none of these issues can be resolved without international co-operation.
I would first like to refer to the disarmament and arms control, because this is an issue of vital importance to all Canadians. 1 would like to begin by reminding the House that Canada's security policy has three complementary thrusts. First, we seek deterrence of war through collective security arrangements of NATO and NORAD. Second, Canada is involved in promoting efforts to achieve equitable and verifiable arms control and disarmament agreements. Third, Canada seeks to support the peaceful settlement of disputes and collective efforts to resolve underlying economic and social issues of international attention. These three goals are clear and unequivocal.
The government remains fully committed to the pursuit of equitable arms control and disarmament measures. The government has advocated and will continue to advocate the negotiation of agreements between the two major nuclear powers to achieve balanced limitations and the reduction of nuclear weapons consistent with common security. This would include binding and verifiable agreements in accordance with the strategy of suffocation put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the United Nations' First Special Session on Disarmament in 1978. The government does not favour a policy of unilateral restraints on the development and deployment of the weaponry of our allies. The strategy of suffocation was never intended to promote self-strangulation.
We attach a great deal of importance to disarmanent and arms control measures. The arms spiral must be broken, and this must begin by meaningful negotiations between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R. The government will take every opportunity to reaffirm the importance it attaches to the continuation of the negotiation process between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R.-
