subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR REVIEWS OF EXTERNAL, DEFENCE AND AID POLICIES
speechtext:
What has happened in the world in the last ten years has been a tragedy of the first order. We can be proud of certain things. Barney Danson, a former minister of national defence, pointed them out in an article in Maclean's magazine. He said that Canada was the first NATO country to relinquish its nuclear capability. He said that we virtually invented peacekeeping, we have contributed heavily to it, and that we spend less of our GNP, 1.7 per cent, on defence than any western alliance except for Luxembourg. We have the most stringent safeguards on the export of armaments and on nuclear power plants, and we have the safest nuclear power plants. But what has happened in this decade? One cannot turn one's eyes away from it. I notice that the NDP is renowned for turning its eyes away and taking specific positions. I do not know if it is for NATO or against NATO, or whether it changes from Wednesday to Wednesday. I really do not know. I hear their party leader saying one thing and I hear their members saying another thing, much like during the debate on the Constitution. I remember they had one seat and the issue was God. They sent one hon. member to support God, one hon. member to speak against God, and the third hon. member to vote on the same issue. It is much the same as what has happened here.
The reality of the world in the last decade is that there has been a Soviet arms buildup. The situation in Afghanistan has occurred. The situation in Poland has occurred. SALT II is now ratified. Our armed forces had been drastically reduced. The situation in Iraq has occurred. Why do we get into nuclear arms? It is because it is cheaper to get into nuclear than conventional arms. Since 1945, there have been 130 wars and 25 million people have died. Isn't that something? We have spoken about World War II and World War I, but there have been 130 wars and 25 million dead. I just recently saw the results of evidence which came from the parliamentary committee mentioned by the hon. member. Even though there are now six countries in the world which have the capability of making a nuclear device, within a decade there will be 44 countries which have that ability. It staggers the imagination. The parliamentary committee did a great service. I think most of its members were more active than I was on that committee, but I must say that the committee did a great service in hearing the evidence, the pros and the cons, and in coming out with balanced and reasonable suggestions. I really do not argue with the suggestions in the minority report because I know that they came from the heart. None of us want what is happening in this world to continue. In the past decade, we have spent $4 million millions on the military. When my secretary typed out my notes, she thought it was a misspelling and only typed in the First million. No one had ever seen $4 million millions, but that is how much we have spent. What are 500,000 of our scientists, 40 per cent of our scientists in the world, doing? They are carrying out R and D for the military.

April 23, 1982
External, Defence and Aid Policies
In 1980, the U.S.A. launched 14 satellites and 89 were launched by the Soviets. What are they doing up there? Forty per cent of these satellites are taking reconnaissance photography. That is ridiculous in the world that we live in. Since 1945, there have been 1,271 nuclear explosions. Who uses up most of the metals and oils in the world? It is the military. Current military spending in the world is $500 million. Anyone who knows anything about spending knows how much is being spent in the world by the military. At the same time we have this going on, 154 countries cannot grow enough food to feed their people. There are 9 million people in the world who cannot buy firewood. The trees we have now are scarce. By the year 2000, half of those will be gone.
In Haiti, one in four children dies before the age of four. This U.N. definition of "absolute poverty" blows the mind. According to that definition, 800 million people in this world live in absolute poverty. Four out of ten children complete more than three years of primary school. Of each ten children born, two die within a year, another dies before five and only five survive to 40, yet around the world we continue to spend $500 million per decade, and that is rising.
I was preparing my notes because I did not know the approach which the hon. member would take. I got to the end of one report, which I think most members have read, and it gives some comparison. Numbers do not mean much if you are not in the military. Megatons or warheads do not mean much, but Hiroshima has some meaning. We have some idea of the size of Hiroshima.
John Gellner, the editor of Canadian Defence Quarterly, estimates that the United States now has 9,500 warheads, which means nothing, equal to 3,500 megatons, which means nothing, which is equal to 200,000 Hiroshima bombs. I repeat that, 200,000 Hiroshima bombs. The U.S.S.R. has 8,000 warheads, which means nothing, equal to 7,800 megatons, which means nothing, equal to 430,000 Hiroshima bombs. Even France, which I had not thought of as a major nuclear power, has 4,700 Hiroshima bombs.

speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member. It is scary and stupid. I agree with what Mr. Danson says. He says we have much to be proud of as Canadians. I apologize for nothing, as far as our aims are concerned. But the hon. member is absolutely right. This debate, this House and this country mean nothing unless we come to grips with the problem of disarmament in this world.
I will end with this bulletin. It was very significant to me. I will not change a word. It is from the February 1980 Disarmament Bulletin. It reads:
The world's military budget equals the annual income of 1,800,000,000 people in the 36 poorest nations.
In two days the world spends on arms the equivalent of a year's budget for the United Nations and its specialized agencies.
The developed nations spend 20 times more for their military programs than for economic assistance to the poorer countries.
The developing nations import arms at the rate of more than $6 billion a year.
The U.S. and U.S.S.R. together account for 60 per cent of the world's military expenditures and for 75 per cent of the world's arms trade; they have more military force than all other nations combined.
Although first in military strength, the superpowers rank lower than many other nations in indicators of social well-being.
World military expenditures average $14,800 per soldier; public expenditures for education $230 per school-age child.
The cost of one Trident submarine equals the cost of a year's schooling for 16,000,000 children in developing countries.
The $80 billion a year spent on arms procurement makes munitions one of the largest industries in the world.
I have to laugh when I see what is coming out of Sweden. At one time they were making grandiose statements. I had no idea of the great arms dealer Sweden has become.

speechtext:
I say to the hon. member, it has nothing to do with socialism. It has much to do with profit and greed. I continue the quote:
Military and space research together get more public research funds than all social needs combined.
The cost of the existing stockpile of weapons in the world is estimated at more than twice the value of the capital stock of all manufacturing industry in the United States.
Quite frankly, I do not accept what the hon. member says about laying down everything we have because there is not much more we can lay down in Canada. The last I saw, the natural resources of Ontario involved a larger amount than the budget of the navy and air force of Canada. We do not have that much left to lay down, but I accept the hon. member's sentiment. Her sentiment is one that has to prevail in the world or there will be no more world. We cannot talk of nations anymore. With all that devastating fire power, it cannot be nation A against nation B or nations A and B against nation C. Dag Hammarskjold said correctly in 1955 at Stanford University:
The question is not either the nation or the world it is, rather, how to serve the world by service to our nation and how to serve the nation by service to the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary started off well. However, he got lost in the field of nuclear or molecular and came up with all sorts of horror stories. I did not quite know where he was going. Perhaps he was just filling in time.
I take seriously the proposition put forward by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett). As she said, the motion has been on the Order Paper for almost two years. I am not clear in my mind, but I think she leaned toward the notion of a special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence or perhaps a special committee, maybe joint with the other place, although probably not, coming as it did from her. I suppose she may want a travelling circus driving across Canada.
April 23, 1982

She has not given full credit to some of the institutions in Canada which provide a forum for the discussion of matters of foreign policy, defence and foreign aid policies, mainly the Canadian Institute of International Affairs from which we hear from time to time. I hope all members of the standing committee are members of that institute.
Parliamentary debate would not do. I suspect there would be barely time in the period allotted to an opposition party to have a parliamentary debate on the matter in one day. Even a long day is not enough. My impression is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would be rather opposed to this because it encroaches upon the area in which he feels he is the expert. He claims to have been the expert for the 14 years plus a few days.
I recall vividly the creation of a special foreign policy division within the prime ministerial office very shortly after he assumed that office. It gradually destroyed any creative initiative. It adversely affected the creative initiative of the foreign service then in place. It was not only on foreign policy matters. He cast off the members of the Department of External Affairs by saying "I can read a much better account in The New York Times the next day. Why do we send these people abroad?" I think he was doing one of the great members of the Canadian Public Service a great disservice. This also happened in CIDA. I could tell some horror stories of CIDA when it set out to operate on its own in complete disregard of the local representatives of Canada. It was in my experience, and I am sure it happened in the experience of others.

The minority report which she and a number of others decided to issue was admittedly given greater attention in the press than the principal report. But that was simply because it was a minority report, not because of its content but because some members ventured to differ from the majority. That was a report on disarmament and security, with a certain amount of emphasis on security.
We were talking about the cost of a Trident submarine perhaps enabling 16 million children to be educated in a year. Has it ever occurred to you that perhaps a Trident submarine is just making it possible for 16 million children to be educated? It is just possible that in the absence of that submarine these 16 million children would not be educated in the manner in which we would like.
Let us balance this. I am glad the parliamentary secretary mentioned that we are a middle power. Some of us develop grandiose notions about the influence we as Canadians have on
External. Defence and Aid Policies
the international scene. When we go abroad on holidays or on missions and are greeted as great Canadians, that is because we do not have an axe to grind. We interpret that as meaning that they think we are great, influential people who can help them. That is a misleading interpretation of the obvious welcome which foreigners have for us. We do not have the clout. Let us face it and be modest about it. Let us not get a swelled head about our influence in the foreign field. With a good foreign service we should be in a position to inform the government as to what is developing in foreign countries. It has been asked why Canada did not engage in an intermediary role. How do you "intermediarize" in a situation where there is a declared aggressor who takes over someone else's territory? It is difficult to take part, because they end up in positions from which it is difficult to back down, particularly when they are in a rather delicate position at home as the Argentinians are.

However, that should not be carried over into the whole international community with the notion that Canada is the great middleman, the fixer for all international crises. We were not very effective in doing anything about Afghanistan and we have not been able to do much about the Argentine, either.
We should have a more thorough examination than the estimates permit, in the field of external affairs, in these particular matters. For example, I tried to get the McDougall report referred to that committee so that we might examine it. The committee needs to be restructured, and that may be what is at the back of the hon. member's suggestion. Then what they decide will have a bearing on government policy. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important to inject into this debate some real facts of life about NATO and the very difficult international circumstances with which NATO is faced at the present time. The members of NATO have their own internal problems as well.

April 23, 1982
External, Defence and Aid Policies
It is fair to say that in spite of all the talk, nothing has been done. Every effort has been made by the North Atlantic Assembly, the members of parliament from 15 countries who meet twice a year to try to promote disarmament and at the same time maintain security. That may seem like a two-edged sword, but it really is not. If you do not maintain security you have absolutely no bargaining power to carry out disarmanent. That is a key point which must be remembered in this debate.
With regard to nuclear force, modernization and arms control, the issue in 1979 was simply to meet the Soviet threats which had then emerged. NATO embarked on a program to modernize the nuclear forces assigned to the alliance in Europe. We have heard a lot about those forces in Europe and the forces among the population that have been opposing nuclear force.
I heard an excellent speaker on the podium in an address in Munich. It was a military person who said that many people think that the military are out to kill, to create war. He said that is absolutely not the intention of the military, because they would be the first persons in the firing line. He said he was wearing that uniform in order to retain peace in the world through a balance of power, so that foreign relations in various countries would have some bargaining power. He said that the military community was the last one that would want to go to war. He did not like being called a warmonger.
I think it is very important that the views of Canadian armed forces personnel or personnel of any other force within the NATO alliance be represented clearly in this debate. They are peacemakers. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Irwin) has just stated that there has been a number of skirmishes since 1945, but in all fairness I think it must also be said that major forces to retain peace in the world since 1945 have been the United Nations and, certainly, NATO.
After two years of study of nuclear rearmament in Europe, on December 12, 1979, NATO decided to proceed with a program to modernize the United States theatre nuclear forces assigned to the alliance in Europe, in part to counter the massive and continuing build-up of new Soviet theatre nuclear forces. The Soviet program involves principally the mobile, triple-warhead SS-20 missile of which at least 250-with a total of 750 warheads-are now operationally deployed. There have been many more since the paper to which I am referring was written. The Russian program is continuing at the rate of more than one new missile each week. The NATO program envisages the deployment, beginning in late 1983 at the earliest, of 108 Pershing 2 missiles, replacing-not adding to- an equal number of old Pershing 1 missiles now deployed in Germany, and the introduction of 464 ground-launched Cruise missiles in Britain, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Italy. For each new nuclear warhead thus introduced an old one will be withdrawn, so that there will be no increase in the NATO stockpile. This is contrary to much of the thinking today.
When deciding to proceed with this program, NATO simultaneously decided to offer to engage the Soviet Union in
arms control negotiations to limit the number of these new weapons on both sides. Here again I want to emphasize the role of NATO in pursuing the aim of getting the major nuclear powers in the world to sit down and talk common sense about the future of humanity, therefore playing a peaceful role rather than that of some great enemy to the public out there trying to create military problems in the world. NATO is there to solve those problems. This was a sincere and reasonable proposal NATO put forward, particularly given the fact that none of the projected new NATO weapons would become available for at least three years. Nevertheless, what did the Soviet Union say? The Soviet Union rejected the offer to sit down for consultations, maintaining that the NATO decision had "destroyed the basis for negotiations". NATO was not going to start replacing its old nuclear weapons until 1983, but the Soviets are going ahead with more than one new SS-20 triple-warhead missile per week. The Russians were saying that they would negotiate if NATO cancelled, or at least suspended, its program. Where would it place NATO if it suspended its program or delayed it altogether for five years or so while at the same time the Warsaw Pact is going ahead and continuing to rearm every week which goes by? NATO would be losing negotiating power because there would no longer be a balance of power to carry on any sensible discussions.
The final result of it all was an announcement following in Haig-Gromyko meeting in New York in September of 1981 which confirmed that the U.S.A. and the Soviet Union agreed to begin theatre nuclear force arms control talks on November 30 last year in Geneva. We now hope those talks will get underway again and continue.
In the few minutes remaining I want to say a few words about our Canadian Department of National Defence. The motion before the House calls for a full parliamentary review of Canada's external, defence and aid policies to redefine Canada's objectives in these areas. I will speak about the defence aspects of the motion.
Canada's defence objectives, like its foreign policy objectives, have been remarkably constant over the past several decades. The principal defence objectives can be simply stated as, first, the prevention of nuclear war; second, the deterring of any conflict which might lead to nuclear war; and, third, the protection of Canadian national interests.
These objectives are as valid today as they were ten years ago, and the government sees no need to review or redefine them at this time. While these objectives have not changed and are unlikely to need change in the foreseeable future, the policies adopted by the government to meet these objectives have been, and must continue to be, dynamic in nature to respond to changing threats, circumstances and priorities.
The protection of Canadian interests and all that implies for the safeguarding of our constitutional process, the protection of our territory and our right to exercise jurisdiction and our ability to enforce our laws is an objective which must be met by Canada alone. We cannot, however-nor can any other
April 23, 1982

single nation in the world-achieve the objectives of preventing nuclear war and deterring conflicts which might lead to such a war strictly on our own. It has to be in co-operation with others. Nor can Canada, given its geographic position between the United States and the Soviet Union and its external interests, prudently follow a neutral or non-aligned foreign policy. Let us not kid ourselves; if there were a nuclear war between the United States and Russia, where would Canada sit geographically?

We are right in between, so to worry about trying to persuade one of our neighbours not to test in Canada equipment-which has no nuclear weapons on it at all-is a poor way to carry on the kind of co-operation we must have within NATO and among NATO countries.
It is the view of the government that, given the economic and political constraints on a middle power such as Canada the only prudent course to achieve our defence objectives is to promote political reconciliation to ease the underlying causes of tension. We have done that with our peacekeeping missions, and the Canadian Armed Forces are well known as some of

the finest diplomats we have sent abroad. We must work for equitable and verifiable arms control agreements. We have done that, we are still doing it and will continue to do it. And we must contribute to collective defence arrangements which will provide a system of stable mutual deterrence. Again 1 must say that without that deterrence we have no bargaining power to bring about any realistic discussions about the reduction of theatre nuclear forces in Warsaw Pact or among NATO nations. We must bargain from a position of strength, and that strength must come from a united group of NATO countries which must retain its strength so that the western powers are in a position to negotiate effectively with the Warsaw Pact to bring about future continued peace in the world.
